VERNON L. GORDON
In future generations, as Masonic historians peruse the Proceedings of
the !31st Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, it is hoped that
in the brief space allotted to the Grand Master's biography, they will
receive a deeper insight and intimate knowledge of the Most Worshipful
Vernon L. Gordon .
"Freemasonry is a growing idea. It can only expand itself to the limits
of the moral and spiritual growth of its individual members." This was the
thread of thought that Brother Gordon wove throughout the fabric of his
term of office. As a prominent figure in the agricultural community of the
San Joaquin Valley, he fully realized that as the tiller of the soil plants,
nurtures and harvests his crop, so does the Master Mason toiling in the
quarries of our Craft, bring to fruition the realization that Masonry is a
way of life.
Our 114th Grand Master first saw the light of day on June 10, 1928 in
Bixby, Oklahoma and shortly thereafter his family moved westward. He
received his education in the public schools of Arizona, and it was in Ho
Ho Kam Chapter of the International Order of DeMolay that our distinguished Bro.ther first experienced the spirit of fraternalism based upon
Masonic teachings.
Brother Gordon's success in life was made certain when in Tranquillity,
California, on August 26, 1949, he was united in marriage with Flora Mae
Reece. She took her place as a loving companion and was the heartbeat
of an inspiring family life, a place she has held with true womanly grace
and charm. In the hearts and minds of California Masons, Mae has truly
epitomized the one who should be the first lady of California Masonry.
They have been blessed with a daughter, Sarah, and a son, David, who
incidentally is also a member of the Order of DeMolay.
During the early 1950's, our Grand Master served his country in Korea
as a member of the Military Police Corps. Upon returning home, his civic
mindedness prompted him to assist in the formation of the Tranquillity
High School Boosters Club over which he subsequently presided as president . His devotion to the principles of public education was recognized
by the members of his community when they elected him several times as
a member of the Tranquillity Union High School Board of Education .
Brother Gordon's service to public education was greatly expanded when
he was appointed to the Fresno County Committee on School District
Organization and thereafter to a position as Director of the Fresno County
School Trustees Association.
Brother Vernon is a member of the Tranquillity United Methodist
Church and serves as a member of the Governing Board as Director of
Finance. This faithful stewardship to his community and his church is a
direct result of his commitment to the principle frequently shared with his
Brethren which is to "learn well first the routine of your task, and then
apply yourself to the full extent of your God-given ability."
Vernon L. Gordon was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason

in Joppa Lodge No. 508 on March 7, 1956 and thence began our Grand
Master' s zealous activities in the vineyards of Masonry.
Twice he served as Master of his Lodge, in 1961 and again in 1965. In
1967 the then Grand Master, Most Worshipful Larry Dayton , appoint ed
him as the Inspecto r of the 414th Masonic District. He served in this
capacity with distinction and seven years later, in 1974, he was designa ted
by Most Worshipful Raymon d A. Ebbage as the Assistant Grand Lecture r
for Division IV. He has also been a member of the Grand Lodge Committee on Distribution and the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California.
In his travels through out our Jurisdiction his firm handclasp and ready
smile, his humility and sincerity, won for him the acclaim and admiration
of his Brethre n. Accordingly, they elected him Junior Grand Warden in
1976. Progressing through the "chairs," on Octobe r 11, 1979 he was installed as Grand Master and was presente d with a gavel fashioned by the
hands of his son, a gavel that was destined to be wielded through out his
term with dignity and fraternal love.
Brother Gordon received the 32° in the Scottish Rite Bodies of Fresno,
and at the Supreme Council Sessions of 1977 he was elected to be coroneted with the 33°. He is presently the Junior Warden of the Lodge of
Perfection and also the Assistant Chairm an of the Sovereign Grand Commander 's Advisory Council. He is also a membe r of Tehran Shrine Temple
of Fresno.
Brother Vernon's concern ed interest and labor on behalf of our Masonic
Youth Organizations was recognized by his being awarded the Grand
Cross of Colors in 1976 and the DeMolay Active Legion of Honor in
1977.
Mae and Vernon are active members of Venus Chapter No. 534, Order
of Eastern Star and on three occasions our Grand Master served his
Chapte r as Worthy Patron, in 1962, 1974 and in 1975.
Our retiring Grand Master can look back with pleasure at the designs
he drew upon the trestleb oard. His Grand Master's Seminars and his 18
Point Program of Proficiency and Appreciation have afforded him the
opportu nity to witness a rebirth of Masonic enthusia sm in the Constit uent
Lodges. He fully realized that everything that can or should be done
cannot be accomplished in one tenn of office, but his philosophy of "why
wait until tomorro w" has given the Masons of this Grand Jurisdiction a
foundat ion stone upon which they may build.
To know Vernon L. Gordon personally is to realize that in him our
Fratern ity has the embodi ment of all that goes to make up a truly good
man, a good citizen, a good husband and a good father..... one whom
we are proud and privileged to call "My Brother."

ONE HUNDRED THIRTY-FIRST
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California commenced its One Hundred Thirty-first Annual Communication in the California Masonic Memorial Temple, San Francisco,
California on Monday, October 13, 1980, A.L. 5980, at 10:00 A.M. Grand
Lodge was raised by Ray Whitaker, Master of Joppa Lodge No. 508 along
with Melvin D. Hughes, a Past Master of that Lodge. The gavels which
were used during the Morning Session were presented to the Grand Master
at his installation in October, 1979 by his son David and by Gordon
Vaughan, Inspector of the 414th Masonic District in memory of Edwin C.
Johnson, a Past Master of Joppa Lodge No. 508. Other gavels used were
presented by Georgetown Lodge No. 25, Lodi Lodge No. 256 and West
Covina Lodge No. 758. Upon the call of the roll, the following elected
and appointive officers responded:

Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
Scripture Reading from the First Chapter of the Second Book of Samuel.
Now it came to pass as David abode in the city, that, behold, a man
came out of t~e camp from Saul, with his clothes rent, and earth upon his
head: and so 1t was, when he came unto David that he fell to the earth
and did obeisance. And David said unto him F;om whence comest thou?
And he said, Out of the camp of Israel. And David said unto him, Ho~
went the matter? .I pray thee, tell me. And he answered, Many of the
people are fallen m the battle; and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead
also. Then David took hold on his clothes, and rent them; and likewise
all ~he men that were with him; and they mourned, and wept and fasted
unttl even, for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of the
Lord; because they were fallen by the sword.
And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan
his son:

Thy Glory, 0 Israel, is slain upon thine high places!
How are the mighty fallen!
Tell it not in Gath,
Publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon·
Lest the daughters of the Philistines rej~ice,
And the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.
Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew
Nor rain upon you, 0 ye fields of death!
'
For th~re was the shield of the mighty viley cast away,
The shield of Saul, as of one not annointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain,
From the fat of the mighty,
The bow of Jonathan turned not back
And the sword of Saul returned not e:ripty.
Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives
And in their death not divided:
'
They were swifter than eagles,
They were stronger than lions.
Ye daughters of Israel weep over Saul,
Who clothed you in scarlet delicately,
Who put ornaments of gold upon your apparel; weep and say,
How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle!
0 Jonathan, slain upon thine high places!
I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan!
Very pleasant hast thou been unto me:
Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of woman.
How are the mighty fallen,
And the weapons of war perished!

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

"O Jonathan, slain upon thine high places!
I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan!
Very pleasant hast thou been unto me:
Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of woman."
Across the distance of the centuries comes a portrait of brotherhood .
There was a shepherd boy. And there was a king's son. It was the king
who brought them together. Saul was a man whose inner life was deeply
troubled. David, the shepherd, played wondrously upon the harp. His
music brought peace to the king. David joined the king's household. And
the king's son, Jonathan, became his friend. Together they played. Together they studied. They shared each other's secrets. They shared each
other's trust. By ties that were stronger than blood, they were brothers.
But Saul grew jealous of David. In time, to protect his life, David left
the royal court. Yet neither time nor distance diminished brotherly love.
And the tragic civil war touched it not. David mourned: "I am distressed
for thee, my brother Jonathan!"
As David and Jonathan were brothers, so were Damon and Pythias, so
through the centuries have men chosen brotherhood.
Look squarely at the present! Brotherhood is a bumper sticker! Brotherhood is a word trotted out once a year by the shoddy variety of politicians! Brotherhood is a word mouthed again and again void of content,
void of meaning!
Again look squarely at the present! You and I have chosen for ourselves
to be brothers. We have chosen brotherhood! At a given moment in our
lives, each of us, "of our own free will and accord," at the altar chose
brotherhood.
What does it•mean to us-this word, this experience? Is it just a formality? Is it just the special word which tells the world that we belong to
a charming clique or prestigious club? Or is it a title by which we address
one another? An empty title?
Look around you. Behold the men who are assembled here in this vast
Lodge room. They are your Brothers. You are theirs. This relationship
exists not because of some Masonic law but because it is Masonic experience.
The times in which we live demand of us that this Masonic experience
be alive and flourish! The times demand of us brotherhood - not as a
token but as a reality.
You reach out your open hand to greet a fellow Mason whom you call
Brother. Your moment of testing is upon you. Is your heart in your action?
Will your love prevent your differences from destroying your friendship?
Brotherhood implies friendship! Brotherhood implies understanding!
Brotherhood implies helpfulness! Brotherhood implies trust!
Brethren, if Freemasonry is to continue to be an influence for freedom
and morality in this our world, we here must live as Brothers.
In a few moments we shall take time to remember those who have
gained admission "into the Celestial Lodge above where the Supreme
Grand Master of the Universe forever presides." In truth, brotherhood

knows no time but reaches through the generations, deep into the past,
distant into the future. But of those Brethren who have touched our lives,
it is fitting that we hold especially tender memories. Not long ago I wrote
a poem which I titled "Instructions." As a tribute to my Brother Masons,
the living and the dead, I now present it to you:
When I have moved beyond you in the adventure of life
gather in some pleasant place
and there remember me with spoken words old and new
Let a tear fall if you will
but let a smile come quickly
for I have loved the laughter of life. . .
Do not linger too long with your solemnities ...
Go eat and drink and talk
and when you can
follow a woodland trail
climb a high mountain
sleep beneath the stars
swim in a cold river
chew the thoughts of some book which challenges your soul
use your hands some bright day
to make a thing of beauty
or to lift someone's heavy load
and, on a special night, in the quiet of the Lodge,
lead some young man to the rule and guide of the square
and compass .. .
Though you mention not my name
though no thought of me crosses your mind
I shall be with you
for these have been realities of life to me .. .
And when you face some crisis with anguish
when you walk alone with courage
when you choose your paths of right
when you give yourself in love
I 'Shall be very close to you ...
I have followed the valleys
I have climbed the heights of life.
Necrology
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Once again as we look back over the year just passed, we are saddened
by the ravages the grim reaper has made in our ranks . We are reminded
of the words of Solomon embodied in our ritual, "Man that is born of a
woman is of few days and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a flower
and is cut down; he fleeth also as a shadow and continueth not."

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

"Solemn strikes the funeral chime." How many tender memories these
old familiar words evoke in the mind of a Mason. Often in open Lodge,
alas, all too often beside the grave, he has heard them march with slow,
majestic step to the measure of the Pleyel Hymn. Never were words and
melody more fittingly blended. Whether we hear this hymn in the tiled
recesses of the Lodge, or on a green sward out under the sky, our hearts
answer to its appeal.
As we walk in memories' hall, we recall the many virtues of our departed Brethren and grieve for the fellowship that we shall enjoy no more.
The roster of our departed members is a roll of honor. Some have served
as business, civic or community leaders; some in government, some in the
military; others in the field of education, the judiciary and many other
vocations, but most of all we honor them for their labors in the vineyards
of Masonry.
Your Committee wishes it might include in this report even a brief
statement of the accomplishments of these Brethren who have so freely
and unselfishly given of their time to promote that spirit of amity and
good will which should characterize those who bear the title of Mason.
The statistics of our report are overwhelming. Death has called from
our midst the largest number in the history of this Grand Lodge. Each is
worthy and entitled to his individual eulogy. All kept alive the imagery of
Masonry in California and Hawaii and maintained standards of integrity,
brotherly love, charity and truth so essentially necessary in this modern
age. Their many deeds would fill more pages than can be allotted to our
use. Their individual names will be inscribed in the printed record of our
Annual Communication.
Five hundred fifteen (515) Past Masters, Masters and Wardens have
crossed the land from whose bourne no traveller returns. "The brittle
thread which bound them to earth has been severed and their liberated
spirits have winged their flight to the unknown world."
Three hundred thirty-six (336) of our Lodges suffered losses. Two
Lodges lost six (6) each, two Lodges lost five (5) each, six Lodges lost
four (4) each, twenty-five Lodges lost three (3) each, ninety-three Lodges
lost two (2) each, and two hundred eight Lodges lost one (1) each.
And so we take leave of our departed Brethren for a time, knowing
they have but passed beyond the horizon of mortal eyes into immortality,
trailing clouds of glory behind as they go, and that "the Supreme Grand
Master shall preserve their going out and their coming in from this time
forth and even for evermore."
A poet has said that the leaves fall fast in Vallombroa, but they are
nothing compared to the human laws that fall daily from the tree of life.
Life is so uncertain that every poet, every philosopher, every Holy Book
of every great religion has dealt with the mystery, attempting in some way
to give comfort and consolation to those who remain.
How comforting indeed must these cheering words of the Psalmist have
been to the hearts of those members of this Grand Lodge who, since the
period covered by our last report, have laid aside the cares and vexations
of this life, and placing their trust in the Supreme Grand Master, have

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

gone to partake with Him the everlasting joys of that existence, the
sweetness of which can only be experienced by those who have entered
into it through the valley of the shadows whose very darkness is but the
harbinger of the coming perfect day.
We who remain will not mourn for our Brethren who have preceded us
but look hopefully forward to the time when they shall greet us as we
emerge from the valley of the shadows into the glorious sunshine of the
presence of the most High, who doeth all things well.
It's hard to lose the ones we love,
To see them pass away,
The sweetest and the kindest gone,
While others are left to stay.
But if we had a flower garden
With roses fair and bright,
We'd often pick the loveliest,
And think it to be right.
And so it is with the Great Architect of the Universe
In His lovely garden here,
He often picks the fairest flower,
The one we love so dear.
The flowers that are pick~d by Him
Will never fade away:
They'll live forever and a day.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

AFTERNOON SESSION-M onday, October 13, 1980
Grand Lodge was called on at 1:30 P.M., the Grand Master presiding.
This session was raised by Eugene Weber, Master of East Belt Lodge No.
391, using the gavel he crafted and presented to the Grand Master. Other
gavels used during this session were presented to the Grand Master by
Orosi Lodge No. 383, Las Palmas Lodge No. 366 and the Los Nietos
Shrine Club.
The Grand Chaplain invoked the blessing of God.

My Brethren:
The Masonic Grand Lodge Year of "Freemasonry - A Growing Idea"
has reached its terminal growth, and whether or not it has produced a
satisfactory harvest can only be judged by He who created the world and
all ~ings therein. All others can only speculate.
In conformity with the usages of the Craft, it is my duty to render an
account of my own stewardship from October 11, 1979 to the present
moment. It has been a busy and gratifying year.
At the 1976 Annual Communication , when I was elected Junior Grand
Warden, I dedicated my service, as an Elective Grand Lodge Officer, to
the memory of Herbert H. Huebner, Wallace H. Fiske, Edwin C. Johnson
and Clarence L. Fraser. Each of these Brothers, in his own way, played
an important part in the shaping of my Masonic life. I pray at this moment
that they would be charitable in their appraisal of the result.
Each of you, my Brethren of the Grand Lodge, made it possible for me
to occupy the high office of Grand Master of Masons in California and
Hawaii, and to each of you I t~nder my heartfelt thanks.
There is much personal satisfaction, to be sure, in holding the highest
office of this Jurisdiction; however, I have consistently stated throughout
this year that he who assumes the glamour of the title, and loses the grace
of humility, will in the end serve only himself. In short, "Let he who
would proclaim himself superstar, do so in the presence of his Creator,
for we common men are unable to see beyond his mortal self."
The story of Freemasonry is written by the efforts of individuals, each
contributing his God-given best, whether it be chapter or verse, and then
combining them together to make the complete volume of our great
brotherhood.
So it has been this year. We have not grown in number, but the renewed
efforts of many dedicated Masons in our Jurisdiction has indeed caused
Freemasonry to flourish as "a growing idea." ·
GENERAL CONDITION OF MASONRY

The never ending cry of declining membership has prevailed again this
year, and with some justification if you are content to deal with numbers.
It should be pointed out, however, that every Lodge that has a declining
membership had exactly the same number of members on its rolls at
another point in time. That it was on a course of growth at that time is
incidental. The fact is, it had enough members to accomplish its Masonic
purpose then, and it has enough to do the same today. Each Lodge has
but to develop the greatest potential of its members, regardless of the
number, and Freemasonry will continue to flourish as it has done for over
six centuries.
To this end we have presented the Lodges with programs that can, and
will, if properly administered, stimulate new excitement and interest in
Freemasonry.

Laymens Program. It has always been my thought that the word "laymen" is a misnomer for this program, in that the strict interpretation of
the dictionary defines this word as, "non-clergy or non-professional."
Within the scope of this interpretation I have never in all of my Masonic
travels met a "lay-Mason," or for that matter a "lay non-Mason ." To
more properly express my own ideas of the intent of the program, I named
it the "Fellowship Program." The change of name has not diminished its
effectiveness; rather it is now a Committee with its own identity and has
grown tremendously as a result.
HAWAIIAN ISLANDS

The memorable visitation to the Lodges of the Hawaiian Islands was
most enjoyable, and it can be truly said that the accomplishments of that
group, in the field of entertainment and hospitality, is unsurpassed in the
Masonic world and elsewhere. I need not mention here all that was done
for my enjoyment. It is sufficient to say that the glowing terms used by
my predecessors to pay tribute to the Brethren of the Islands were none
too lavish, and they deserve all the compliments that have heretofore
been bestowed upon them.
I am convinced that the leadership in this beautiful outpost of California
Freemasonry will continue to work for the preservation of the highest
level of fraternal participation. Your Grand Master, this year, permitted
the Committee for the study of the feasibility of an Hawaiian Grand
Lodge to continue their painstaking work. It is hoped that the incoming
Grand Master will extend their authority through 1981 under the existing
guidelines.
VISITATIONS OUT OF THE JURISDICTION

I traveled out of the Jurisdiction on three occasions this year. with the
first being the Grand Master's Conference in Washington, D. C., in February. The Masonic fellowship and exchange of ideas, experienced in the
casual hours of the Conference, are most helpful from a fraternal relations
standpoint; however, the formal meetings of the Conference, in my opinion, are not productive and would not justify the expense if that was all
there was to it. All of the widely known problems are raised, but with
little or no direction toward a solution.
In March of this year the Grand Master, along with a large delegation
of California Masons, traveled to La Paz, Baja California, for a Conference with the leaders and members of the Grand Lodges of Baja California North and Baja California South. The meetings were both industrious

INSURANCE PROGRAM

At the 1979 Annual Communication, the Grand Master was directed
by vote of the Grand Lodge, to appoint a Committee to study the formation of a consortium of Constituent Temples for the purpose of combining forces in the area of insurance programs, and perhaps other desirable purposes. I must confess that as Deputy Grand Master, I was either
out of the Lodge Room, or missed the motion entirely, and as a result did
not become aware of the same until early spring. The Committee was
appointed at that time and has been working all out to accomplish its
assignment. I am confident that a report will be made at this session.
GENERAL ACTIVITIES OF THE GRAND MASTER

Past Grand Master Donald G. Ingalls left me with two Recommendations, and I trust that I have fulfilled each to his expectations.
The first was the continuation of the Special Committee to Study the
Organizational Structure of Grand Lodge. In October of last year I reappointed the Cqmmittee as it was previously struct1:1red and pledged to
them not only my personal support but also the assistance of the Grand
Master's office to its fullest extent. The Committee has performed in such
manner as will give highest prise to its members, and to a grateful Fraternity. My personal thanks to each of them.
The Second Recommendation suggested the continuation of the Grand
Master's Seminars in some form. I am happy to report that the Grand
Master's Seminars, 1980, were held in each of the six Divisions and were
highly successful. The entire Elective Progressive Line formed the panel
at each Seminar, and the results were equally educational for the Elective
Officers as for the members in attendance. By our personal contact with
so many members, we were able to have greater insight as to what you
want your Fraternity to be, and the direction you would like it to go. My
personal thanks to the Assistant Grand Lecturers for their assistance in
these programs.
There were many outstanding events during the year, and it would be
impossible to mention all of them. To mention just a few, I had the honor,
jn February of this year, to present the first Masonic Presidential Award
to Brother Mason, and former President, Gerald R. Ford. Brother Ford
was most gracious in his acceptance of the Award, and it must be termed
a great moment for Freemasonry in California.

It has been the accepted custom for the Senior Past Grand Master,
either in the North or the South, to assume Chairmanship of the Committee on an informal basis, and I must admit, with a fairly high degree
of success. It is my belief, however, that the Grand Master is in the best
position to coordinate the activities of the Committee and to govern its
deliberations. It is also my belief that a required quorum is vital in this
most important decision concerning the future of our Grand Lodge.
It is, therefore, my Recommendation No. 1 that the second paragraph
of Section 200 be deleted and substituted with the following:
"The Grand Master, the Past Grand Masters and three members of this
Grand Lodge to be appointed annually by the Grand Master to serve for
a single term only and concurrently with the term of the appointing Grand
Master and who are not past or present Elected Grand Officers, shall
constitute a Committee to recommend to the Grand Lodge a member
thereof for election as Junior Grand Warden. The Grand Master shall call
such meetings of the Committ~e as are necessary and shall preside thereat,
but shall not vote except as hereafter provided. A majority of the Committee eligible to be present shall constitute a quorum at the meeting at
which the recommendee is selected. A majority vote of those present and
eligible to vote shall be necessary to select the recommendee; however,
in all cases of a tie vote, the Grand Master may have the deciding vote."

GRAND MASTER'S RELIEF FUND

Flood damage in Mississippi during the early part of t~is year resulted
in requests for assistance from the Masons of that area m amounts th.at
were beyond the ability of the Lodges or the Grand Lodge of that Junsdiction to provide.
Preliminary estimates of losses approximated one million dollars, of
which less than ten percent was covered by insurance. A great nuf!lber ~f
our Brother Masons completely lost their homes as well as their businesses. Our Brethren needed a helping hand.
In July, therefore, in response to their urgent request, I aut~orized
payment, by our Grand Lodge, of one thousand dollars toward assistance
of our Brethren there.

Number 2.
The foregoing Recommendation suggests a severe overhaul of Section
200, and for that reason I am hesitant to make further recommendations
in that area; however, I feel that additional comment should be made.
The Deputy Grand Master has over the years, with few exceptions,
advanced to the office of Grand Master. He must, however, maintain a
very tentative position under existing law in planning for that most important year. He must, in making appointments, accepting invitations,
developing programs or planning in general, preface his statements with,
"If I am elected to the office of Grand Master." The Brethren of the
Fraternity are somewhat understanding of this situation; however, the
non-Masonic leaders of many of our public agencies are not in tune with
this kind of an approach.
I believe that our Fraternity would display a more positive and progressive image if the Deputy Grand Master could respond to Mayors,
City Councils, Boards of Supervisors, heads of governmental agencies and
Boards of Education with a firm "Yes, I will accept" and "Yes, we will
perform" attitude.
To assure that it be considered in the most thoughtful manner, I recommend that the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, a Standing
Committee, be instructed to study the feasibility of making the office of
Deputy Grand Master, in fact but not in title. the Grand Master-elect. It

The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language defines it
as: "of, concerning, or affecting the community or the public; the public
good, connected with or acting on behalf of the people, community, or
government, rather than private matters of interest."
Thus, in the broad sense, the definition of the word "public" can
reasonably include organizations or entities other than those chartered as
governmental if their operations are sufficiently broad to fall within the
above stated definitions.
The Columbia Encyclopedia, Second Edition, states that the Red Cross
is an international organization for the alleviation of human suffering and
fhe promotion of public health. The American National Red Cross is
headquartered in Washington, D. C., under a Congressional charter
granted in 1905, and is supported entirely by voluntary contributions.
The President of the United States is Honorary Chairman of the Society
and appoints its president and seven members of its fifty member Board
of Governors. The organization accounts are, or were, audited by the War
Department.
It was my Decision, on December I, 1979, that the San Gabriel Chapter
Headquarters Building of the American Red Cross was a proper building
for a Cornerstone Ceremony. The stone has been laid, and the reporting
of it in such detail is not intended to "open the door" for future ceremonies. Rather, it is intended to strengthen our long standing interpretation of the word "public."

Number 3.
Having performed almost all of the Grand Lodge ceremonies which are
open to the public, I have found a troublesome variance in the policy, if
not the law, regarding the opening of Grand Lodge for such ceremonies.
One ceremony indicates that Grand Lodge may be opened; another is
somewhat silent on the matter; a third directs that it must be opened; and
yet a fourth provides for the opening of Constituent Lodges. This variance
can be confusing for the Grand Master as well as the host Lodges in
scheduling the several events.
After studying the written details of the ceremonies and having performed most of them first hand, I find no reason that would support this
inconsistancy.
It is my Recommendation No. 3 that the Ritual Committee be directed
to change the instructions to read: "Grand Lodge may be opened at all
public ceremonies at the discretion of the Grand Master."
This could be accomplished with a single paste-in sheet on page two of
the Book of Ceremonies.
DECISIONS

Number I.
My first Decision as Grand Master was made, of necessity, even prior
to my election to that office. The question was, "Is it proper to accept an
invitation to, and lay the Cornerstone for a Red Cross Chapter Headquarters Building?" The C.M .C. states in part: "The Grand Master may
officiate at the laying of a Cornerstone for a public building."
California Government Code Section 6300 defines a public corporation
as: " .. the state, any political subdivision thereof, any incorporated municipality therein, any public agency of the state, any political subdivision
therein, or any municipality therein, or any corporate municipal instrumentality of this state .. "
Section 200 of the Evidence Code states:. "Public entity includes a
nation, state, county, city and county, city. district, public authority, public
agency, or any other political subdivision or public corporation, whether
foreign or domestic."
Government Code Section 830 defines "Property of a Public Entity"
and "Public Property" to mean real or personal property owned or controlled by a public entity.
Thus, looking strictly to the Statutory Law of California, the Red Cross
must be a public corporation or entity, as defined, in order for its building
to be a "public building."
In looking at Webster's New International Dictionary, however, we find
"public" defined as: "of or pertaining to the people; relating to, or affecting, a nation, state, or community at large - opposed to private."

25

Number 2.
On March 18th of this year, ten members of various Lodges took a Third
Degree Proficiency examination in Gravel Range Lodge No. 59. The
information provided the Grand Master, indicated that all ten were examined at the same time. In addition, there was no record of a request
for courtesy work by any of the Lodges of the several members involved.
While the C.M.C. does not speak directly to the issue of the Third
Degree Proficiency•. there is sufficient precedent in Section 2668 to govern
the number of applicants that may be examined at one time. I quote from
it: "Any number of applicants may be examined at any meeting, but no
more than five shall be examined at any one time with the questions being
asked in rotation ."
It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge that any courtesy work must
be requested by the member's own Lodge, in that it is the responsibility
of that Lodge to maintain an accurate record thereof.
It was my Decision that the Third Degree Proficiency examination
taken in Gravel Range Lodge No. 59 by ten Master Masons whose names
are recorded in the Gr~nd Secretary's office, be declared null and void.
Number 3.
The California Masonic Code is very specific in Sections 502, 504, 4002
and 4004 regarding the vote required for passage of proposed amendments
to the Constitution or Ordinances of this Grand Lodge. There is a "grey

26

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

area", however; in the determination of the vote required for passage of
those matters which do not purport to change the Constitution or Ordinances.
It is possible that one Grand Master could interpret the word "Resolution," as it is used in Sections 160 and 450 of the C.M.C., to require
that all matters brought before the Grand Lodge should be voted upon in
the manner as provided for in Sections 502, 504, 4002 and 4004 . It is also
possible that another Grand Master, in another year, could rule that
Sections 160 and 450 are not definitive to include matters which do not
purport to change the Constitution or Ordinances. The result could be
that matters of equal importance would not receive equal consideration
in different years.
To clarify the law as it is written, and to eliminate further confusion in
this area, it is my Decision, "That unless otherwise specified by the
California Masonic Code, only a majority vote is required to decide any
question brought before the Grand Lodge."

. The~e are challenging times in Freemasonry, and these are challenging
times m our country. The challenge of our times prompts us to pray with
Josiah G. Holland:

Number 4.
The question has come to me, "May those matters of ritual, not written
into the law of this Grand Lodge, be modified or deleted by a simple
majority vote?"
My answer, as Grand Master, is "no." Section 1114 of the C.M.C.
charges the Grand Lecturer with the responsibility of "requiring conformity with the adopted ritual and work." Likewise, Section 1116 directs
the Assistant Grand Lecturers, "To insure proper instruction to the Officers and strict compliance with the adopted work."
The law further provides in Section 2688 C.M.C.: "Each degree conferred and all lectures in this Jurisdiction must be in conformity with the
ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized by the Grand
Lodge." Section 2690 deals with the change of ritual in this manner: "The
Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize any changes in the ritual for
the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from time immemorial."
While it would be impossible to include all of the ritual of this Grand
Lodge in the California Masonic Code, there is sufficient evidence that
the ritual is deeply imbedded in the Ordinances of this Jurisdiction, and
therefore is a part of the law and to adopt any change is to change the
law itself.
It is, therefore, my Decision that all changes in the ritual shall be voted
upon in the same manner as provided for in Sections 4002 and 4004 of the
C.M.C.
CONCLUSION

In conclusion, let me express my heartfelt gratitude to all of the Masons
of this Grand Jurisdiction for their honest efforts in extending the cause
of Freemasonry to the several limits of the States of California and Hawaii.
We have accomplished much by working with each other, for each other.

"God give us men! A time like this demands
Strong minds, great hearts, true faith, steady ha~ds:
Men whom the lust of office does not kill·
Men whom the spoils of office cannot buy';
Men who possess opinions and a will;
Men who have honor, who will not lie;
Men who can stand before the demagogue
And damn his flattering without winking;
Tall men, sun crowned, who live above the fog
In public duty and private thinking."
This past year I have seen the true working of true Masons-men
dedicated to God and to their fellowmen. These are the Ancient Landmarks of the Craft-the Fatherhood of God, and the Brotherhood of
Man. My own expe~iences through the year convince me more vividly
than ever of the destmy of our great Fraternity.
We are men of faith drawn together in good works by the bonds of
brotherly love. We are men of faith who can, and will, lead the world out
of chaos and despair. We are men of faith, who, because of our great trust
have found an inner resource of quiet strength. Let us not quibble about
creeds, but let us accept the great challenge, "to do justly, to love mercy
and to walk humbly with our Creator."
Let us turn to the tasks that confront us. The tasks that confront us at
this Communication, tasks from every walk of life from which we come
the tasks of ca'using Freemasonry to become "a growing idea" in th~
hearts and minds of all men. Because we are Masons, and because of our
reputation among men, the behavior pattern of our communities is influe.n~~d greatl~ by the way we live. God has laid upon us a great respon~1b1l.1ty and given us a wonderful opportunity to build a society in which
JUSttce, mercy and humble reverence for our Maker are the standards of
behavior. To measure up to that opportunity, He has showed us how to
walk humbly with Him.
May each one of us, as men of faith, re-dedicate ourselves to the task
of building for eternity so that our works will stand the test of time and
bear the marks of a Master Mason. In this endeavor, let us be guided by
the thought of John Ruskin who once said, "When we build, let us think
that we build f~rever. Let it not be for the present delight nor for present
use alone. Let tt be such work as our descendants will thank us for and
let us think as we lay stone on stone, that time is to come when those
stones will be held sacred because our hands have touched them· and that
men will say as they look upon the labor and wrought substance' of them

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
A Third Degree Proficiency examination in Gravel Range Lodge No.
59, in which ten members of various Lodges were examined at the same
time, was declared null and void by Grand Master's Decision No. 2.
Two irregularities were noted by the Grand Master. (1) There was no
record of a request for courtesy work by any of the Lodges of the several
members involved. (2) More than five members were examined at one
time.
Although the California Masonic Code is silent regarding proficiency in
the Third Degree, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees
with the Grand Master that there is sufficient precedent for such examination in the statement in Section 2668, "Any number of applicants may
be examined at any meeting, but no more than five shall be examined at
any one time with the questions being asked in rotation."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes concurs in Decision
No. 2 of the Grand Master and recommends its approval.
The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual concurred in the report of the Policy and
General Purposes Committee and recommended a "YES" vote.
The Grand Master's Decision was approved.

WHEN A MAJORITY VCYTE ONLY IN GRAND LODGE DECIDES

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committe e on Jurisprudence, to which the Grand Master's Decision No. 3 was referred, reports as follows:
The Grand Master has correctly interpreted the Code with respect to
the vote required for passage of legislation not involving amen~ments to
the Constitution or Ordinance s. We therefore move the adoption of the
following Resolution:
"RESOLV ED that the following paragraph be added to Section 160 of
the California Masonic Code between the first and second paragraphs
of said section:
"Except as provided in Sections 502, 504, 4002 and 4004 relating to the
vote required to amend the Constitution and Ordinance s of this Grand
Lodge, the transaction of business in Grand Lodge at its Annual Commupication shall be decided by a majority of the vote."
Since this legislation was not presented to the Grand Secretary at least
90 days prior to the commence ment d~te o.f this Annual Comm.unication,
it must be considered as emergent leg1slat1on pursuant to Section 160 of
the California Masonic Code.
To bring the matter before this Communi cation, we therefore move that
the proposed legislation be considered at this time by this Grand Lodge
as emergent legislation. To carry, this mo~ion requires a 516 vo~e ..
Since this Grand _Lodge voted to consider the matter at this t.t.me, to
place the legislation before you, we move the adoption of the Resolution.
To be adopted, the Resolution requires a 516 vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master in his Decision No. 3 has stated that certain resolutions require only a majority vote. This is a serious question with important consequences for the Grand Lodge.
.
Amendme nts to our Constitution clearly require a 516 vote m the year
the proposed amendmen t is made, or a 2/3 vote if the matter is carried
over to the next year. Amendme nts to our Ordinance s require the same
vote.
Are there propositions before Grand Lodge which do not amend either
the Constitution or our Ordinances? If so, by what percentage of the
ballots cast must the proposition pass?
Nowhere in the California Masonic Code is a majority vote for passage
of Grand Lodge Legislation mentioned. Yet the implication of the requirement of a 516 or 2/3 vote on certain kinds of matters is that if there are
other kinds of matters a lesser vote is required. If such a situation were
to arise during the Annual Communications, the Grand Master would be
required to rule, from which ruling there could be no appeal. (CMC

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Decision No. 4 replies to the question, "May those
matters of ritual, not written into the law of this Grand Lodge, be modified
or deleted by a simple majority vote?"
Noting that the Grand Lodge alone has the power to authorize any
changes in the ritual, the Grand Master concluded that there is sufficie~t
evidence that the ritual is deeply imbedded in the Ordinances of this
Jurisdiction and therefore is a part of the law and to adopt any change is
to change the law itself.
His answer to the question raised, therefore, was "No," and his Decision
was "that all changes in the ritual shall be voted upon in the same manner
as provided for in Sections 4002 and 4004 of the C.M.C."
.
.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes concurs m the Decision No. 4 of the Grand Master and recommends its approval.
The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual concurred with the report of the Jurisprudence Committee.
The intent of the Grand Master's Decision as incorporated in language
proposed by the Jurisprudence Committee and approved by the Grand
Master to amend C.M.C. Section 2690 was Adopted.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

The financial statements of the Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes, Masonic
Memorial Temple and Masonic Foundation, verified by our auditors, Lindquist van Husen and Joyce of San Francisco, are an integral part of this
Grand Treasurer's report. You are urged to carefully read the several
sections as each gives a complete financial picture of your Grand Lodge
and its several entities.
Our law provides that your Grand Treasurer serve as Treasurer of
Masonic Homes, Masonic Memorial Temple and Masonic Foundation
Boards of Trustees. Attendance this past year provided not only the
opportunity to become better acquainted but to more fully understand
. and appreciate the dedicated attention of all Board members.
The reports of these several Boards deserve your attention . It is appropriate here to briefly comment only on their financial condition; without
diluting your interest in the Board chairman's remarks.
Our principal financial activity has to do with the operation of our fine
Homes at Union City and Covina. Again this year, Masons have substantially supported the Homes endowment fund; investment income is now
approximating the operating costs of both Homes; and the Homes Trustees have continued their careful attention to the rehabilitation program
at Union City, expected to be fully complete by the end of this calendar
year. California Masonry can be justifiably proud of their Homes, its high
level of love and care for the elderly and for the children, and, of great
importance, its financial strength and stability.
Your Memorial Temple Trustees will report on another year of successful operation of this fine edifice now in its twenty-second year of use
and occupancy. Their principal concern at this time has to do with necessary expenditures for repairs and refurbishment, all of which is adequately taken care of by established reserves.
Our California Masonic Foundation continues to prosper. A decided
improvement in receipts from bequests and contributions, together with
an improved investment return, allowed the Trustees to continue their
dedicated attention to its charitable purpose, that of granting scholarship
awards to deserving and qualified students. Here is another worthy Masonic charitable activity receiving financial support of Masons and others
throughout our jurisdiction.
A major share of the accounting duties in our Grand Lodge office is
related to our Homes' operations. Accrual accounting requires that more
modern controls be maintained, and improved methods utilized, in order
to furnish timely management data particularly for Board Trustees. There
is good reason to expect that the recent addition of an experienced Comptroller to our Staff will greatly enhance our accounting capabilities, especially in the area of Homes management.
My sincere thanks and appreciation are extended to this Grand Lodge
for the privilege of serving as your Grand Treasurer ; to our Grand Master

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

49

Most Worshipful Vernon L. Gordon and his fellow officers for their confidence and s~pport; and to the office staff in its desire to be ever helpful
and cooperative.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN A. SICKENBERGER, Grand Treasurer

Referred .to Committee on Distribution. Committee on Distribution
referred entire report to Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

In accordance with the requirements of the California Masonic Code
outlining the duties and responsibilities of the Grand Secretary, I have the
pleasure of presenting this, my third annual report as your Grand Secretary.
The Grand Treasurer's report reflects all monies we have received and
released to the Grand Treasurer, all of which has been credited to the
accounts of the several Masonic entities. Each has been audited by the
accounting firm of Lindquist, von Heusen and Joyce. All supporting
books, papers and vouchers are on file in the Grand Lodge office as are
all minutes of meetings of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, the
Memorial Temple Trustees, the Masonic Foundation Trustees and the
Investment Committee. The members and Chairman of the Finance Committee of Grand Lodge, together with appropriate sub-Committees of the
Homes and Memorial Temple Boards, have reviewed applicable receipts
and disbursements and have assisted in matters of budgeting and financial
requirements of each entity.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PERSONNEL

past should ~e adequate to meet t?day's operati.ng expenses. T~is is not
true in most instances. They have fatled to recognize the constant increases
in expenses of Lodge operations caused by inflationary factors outside of
the Fraternity and have seriously handicapped Lodge functions in many
cases by resistance to proposals to upward adjustments in annual dues. It
is urged that each Lodge make an honest and critical review of its own
situation on this matter.

During the past year several new employees were added to our staff,
replacing those who left due to retirement or for other jobs. We have
been able, however, to secure competent people who have a sense of
responsibility to their particular functions and at the same time to understand that our office is service oriented. A good part of their work day is
devoted to service to our membership. We feel fortunate that we have
such a committed staff and can rely on their efficient performance.
Your office has a new controller, Newlon "Dick" Benner, C.P.A. who
started with us in June, to replace Ms. Birma Roush, who for health
reasons took an early retirement in February. We look forward toward
improving and updating our accounting system and records.

MEMBERSHIP

In my report last year, I called attention to the continuing decline in
total membership and the increase in consolidations of Lodges. This last
year has seen no reversal of this trend. On the contrary, the net loss of
membership (4147) is the highest for any single year in the history of the
Grand Lodge. The same is true as it relates to Lodge consolidations.
Again, as for last year, the greatest single cause of loss in membership is
death. It should be noted that during the 1920's our membership more
than doubled, and it is these Brethren who in recent years account for the
large number of deaths.
Of greater concern should be the continuing number of candidates who
do not complete their degree work and ultimately have their fees and
contributions forfeited. It is not expected that every man who applies for
the degrees will become a Master Mason, but when we note that there
are Lodges that have dozens of candidates who have not progressed, we
must conclude that a lack of communication as to the real purposes of
Masonry exists between the Master, the candidates' coaches and the candidates themselves. In our opinion the condition would be helped if each
Master would personally contact every such candidate to determine and
to eliminate the causes and thus, hopefully, bring about a resumption of
their growth in the work.

55

ACCOUNTING RECORDS

Pursuant to C.M.C. Section 1108-5th the transition from a cash basis of
accounting which prevailed for many years to the accrual method has
been completed for the several entities of Grand Lodge and Homes. This
has been done to meet current provisions of our own law, as well as the
standards set out by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants as they relate to financial records and statements of non-profit and
charitable organizations. The change will allow for better analysis of
operating conditions and management of the Fraternity's assets.
At the last Communication we reported that the equipment employed
in our accounting work had then been recently analyzed, and recommendations had been made for installation of different, more effective equipment. Changes of personnel in certain principal positions in our accounting
department which we reported, as well as preliminary excess work required to make changes in our methods have slowed up the effecting of
the mechanical changes. These delaying factors have now been overcome.
Our accounting program will be given first attention for improvement.
Later on membership records will be transferred to data processing equipment. We are confident we will be able to serve the Lodges better when
the installation Is complete.
PARAPHERNALIA

During the year, the old "Southern Traveling Set" of Grand Lodge
Officers' aprons was replaced by a beautiful new set. Combined with the
two new sets acquired last year, your Grand Lodge Officers will now have
appropriate quality regalia for use during the Annual Communication and
for all Grand Lodge openings in both the Southern and Northern areas
of the Jurisdiction . It is important that the appearance of the Grand Lodge
Officers be in keeping with the reputation and dignity of our Fraternity.
SECRETARIES' ASSOCIATIONS

DUES

Elsewhere in this report is a statistical table which sets forth the annual
dues structure of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction. It should be noted that
the average dues in California in the year 1970 were $18.96. The average
dues in 1980 are only $24.75. The members of many of our Lodges persist
in the erroneous view that the dues which have prevailed for years in the

Representatives from our office continue to meet, most often on a
quarterly basis, with various voluntary Secretary Association groups
throughout the State. The groups meet to promote and improve their
mutual interests and work, and the practice has been in existence since
1914. More than 50 such meetings are now held each year. We believe
that a most effective area of service is advanced through contacts afforded
by these meetings. It is our strong conviction that such well attended

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Secretaries' meetings, with open discussion on matters of mutual and
current concern, are more constructive to the Secretaries' and Lodges'
interests than communication through the limitations of correspondence
or telephone calls.
Lodge officers, Inspectors, or any Master Mason who is interested are
always welcome to attend these Association meetings.
We continue to hold in high regard those Brethren who devote so much
of their time and effort to the task of handling the multiplicity of forms,
reports, notices and correspondence which is required of a Lodge Secretary and we appreciate the continuing cooperation received from them.
They are truly "workers" in the vineyards of Masonry.

in mechanical proficiency should be further enhanced by its awareness of
the group's devotion to principle and loyalty to the duties to which each
has been assigned. My particular duties have been substantially lightened
by the assistance of these conscientious, faithful employees who have
made work a pleasure.
Our office will continue in its commitment to serve the Fraternity to
the limit of its capacity through the years for it is easy to do so when
dealing with the Masonic princ;ples of Brotherly love, relief and truth!

56

FILING OF ANNUAL INFORMATION RETURNS

The report of the Taxation Committee will place emphasis upon the
importance of those Lodges and Temple Associations required to do so,
to comply with the Federal and State laws with respect to their filing
annual information returns on a timely basis. Several of our entities last
year incurred severe monetary penalties for failure to comply with the
requirements of the law. In our meetings throughout the State with Lodge
Secretaries, we have repeatedly called their attention to the fact that since
a non-profit, tax exempt status has been granted to us, it is incumbent
upon every Lodge and Temple Association to comply with the provisions
of the law. In addition, each year notification in writing is distributed to
each Lodge reminding the Secretary that the Annual Information returns
must be filed on or before a specified date. We are pleased that most of
them each year fulfill their obligation in this regard. We hope that 100%
compliance will be this year's record.
CONCLUSION

Of necessity, a close working relationship must exist between the Grand
Secretary and the Grand Master in order that the administrative issues
which present themselves periodically during the year may be quickly,
smoothly and amicably resolved. It has been a rare privilege to have been
so closely associated with our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Vernon L.
Gordon. His depth of human understanding and his grasp of procedural
matters has resulted in continued effective functioning of the relationship
between the Grand Lodge office and the office of Grand Master. I am
indebted to this sensitive man and Mason for the valued relationship we
have enjoyed, and I wish him well in his future endeavors.
My appreciation is also extended to all those who continue to provide
our office with their individual expertise-Past Grand Masters, Grand
Lodge Officers, Inspectors, Committeemen and particularly Lodge Secretaries who, on a day by day basis, exemplify the true meaning of
Masonry and strengthen our sense of satisfaction in serving the Fraternity.
The Fraternity can be justifiably proud of the entire staff of the Grand

The applicati on of Tujunga Lodge No. 592 to act upon the applicati on
for degrees of a person belonging to the Armed Forces of the United

The applications of Corinthi an Lodge No. 9 and Elysian Lodge No. 418
to hold an election to fill a vacancy failed to certify that they had been
approved by two-third s of the members present at a Stated Meeting.
The Committ ee calls to the attention of Lodge Secretari es that the seal
of the Lodge is to be affixed to all papers issued under its authority or in
obedienc e to all the requirem ents of the Constitu tion and Regulati ons of
the Grand Lodge, and therefore that all applications for dispensa tions and
attendan t papers must have the Lodge seal affixed to them.
We recomme nd that, except for the five (5) instances , the actions of the
Grand Master be approved , and that in the cases of Huntingt on Beach
Lodge No. 380 and Utopia Lodge No. 537, each Lodge pass a new
resolutio n reflecting the appropri ate minimum payment of money for Life
Members hip required in accordan ce with Section 2804 of the Californi a
Masonic Code, and that in the case of Tujunga Lodge No. 592, the Lodge
be requeste d to furnish proper certification that due notice was given to
each of its members of the meeting at which the ballot on the applicati on
for degrees of a person belonging to the Armed Forces of the United
States who did not possess the qualifications of residence, and that in the
cases of Corinthia n Lodge No. 9 and Elysian Lodge No. 418, each Lodge
be requeste d to furnish proper certification that their applicati on to hold

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:
Your Committee on By-Laws for this Grand Lodge met on Monday,
October 13, 1980, for the purpose of reviewing the various amendments

63

Although ~ot included in the printe~ report, these proposed changes
were also reviewed and, e~cept as herema~ter specifically set forth, they
were found to be adopted m accordance with current Masonic Law.
The Committee, as a result of its review of all matters submitted to it
found all items in order except the following:
'
1) The request of Hanford Lodge No. 279 to increase the fees for the
degrees is ~n error in that the amendment was proposed at the
stated meeting held on September 5, 1979 and was not, as required,
acted upon "at the next stated meeting." The vote instead was held
on November 7, 1979 and thus unless the request was resubmitted .
to the Lodge at the October stated meeting, the action does not
comply with our statutes. In any event, the Certificate of Amend-

64

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ment must be reprepared to reflect the presentation of the proposed
amendment at one stated meeting and a vote taken at the NEXT
stated meeting.
2) The application of Covina Lodge No. 334 to increase its dues erroneously shows the proposed amendment to have been submitted
on August 5, 1980 with the vote thereon having been taken at the
"next stated meeting" held on August 2, 1980. Since the Lodge
holds its stated meetings on the first Tuesday of each month, it
appears that the latter date should properly read September 2,
1980, which was the first Tuesday in September. The Certificate of
Amendment needs to be corrected by the Secretary to reflect the
correct information.
3) A similar error exists in respect to the application of Yerba Buena
Lodge No. 403 for an increase in dues. The Certificate reflects
introduction of a proposed amendment on August 7, 1980 with the
vote taken "at the next stated meeting, held on the 4th day of
August, 1980." It appears that the latter month should read "September" since September 4 is the first Thursday and was the scheduled date for the Lodge's stated meeting. Again a corrected Certificate is needed.
4) The application of El Cajon Valley Lodge No. 576 for a dues
increase likewise discloses that the vote was not taken at the next
stated meeting as required. Correspondence from the Lodge reflects
that the proposed amendment was introduced at the June stated
meeting; discussed at the July stated meeting, at which time the
Master announced that the membership had been notified that the
vote would be taken at the August stated meeting; and at the
August stated meeting the vote was taken. The Certificate is still in
error and must be corrected to reflect compliance with the Code by
showing the amendment introduced (or reintroduced) at the July
stated meeting and a vote taken at the next stated meeting held in
August.
5) The same problem is present in respect to the application of Zenith
Lodge No. 768 for an increase in its dues. The amendment was
presented in September of 1979 and apparently voted on in November 1979 with no explanation. As heretofore stated, the action is
improper and must be corrected. If the matter was reintroduced at
the October 1979 meeting then it can be corrected by the submission
of an amended Certificate from the Secretary showing the correct
dates. Otherwise, the action will have to be taken again. In any
event, the vote must be at the next succeeding stated meeting after
the proposed amendment is shown in the Certificate as having been
presented.
6) A different problem presents itself in respect to the proposed
amendment of Kerman Lodge No. 420 concerning its dues. In
addition to increasing their dues they attempted to require dues to
be paid annually in advance on the first day of January. This is
improper. The Uniform Code of By-Laws, which is to be adopted

by all Lod.ges in this jurisdiction, provides for dues to be "payable
quarter!~. m advance on the first day of January, April, July and
Oc~ober. The Lodge must comply with these provisions of the
Umform Code of By-Laws which is a part of our California Masonic
Code and thus this application cannot be approved in its present
form.
7) The ~pplication of !he Gardens Lodge No. 621 for a change in its
meetmg place requires .co.rrection in ~hat the vote of the Lodge is
not shown. The form ts mcomplete m that it does not show the
number. of members present at the meeting nor the number of
affirmative votes. The application cannot be approved until this
information is provided.
8) Mention must again be made of the failure of the Secretaries to
affix the Lodge Seal on their Certification as required by Section
2076, C.M.C. The following actions all should be returned so as to
have the seal affixed:
a) Re adoption of Uniform Code of By-Laws:
San Francisco Educator Lodge No. 166
Landmark-Buckeye Lodge No. 195
Santa Lucia Lodge No. 302
Cahuenga-La Brea Lodge No. 513

b) Re changing date of stated meeting:
Saddleback Valley Lodge No. 832
c) Re increase in dues:

Approximately one and one-half years ago our Chairman, Worshipful
Harold S. Morrison, was stricken by an ailment which has rendered it
impossible for him to continue his outstanding efforts on behalf of our
Grand Lodge Cpmmittee on Trial Review. His many years of experience
as an Inspector and member and Chairman of our Committee was always
of inestimable value to our Committee and his able counsel and advice
have been sorely missed. Nonetheless, your Committee has continued to
be inspired and uplifted by the experience and guidance he has furnished
to us in the past and we are sure that spiritually he is with us this week
during our Annual Communication. We are pleased to report that Brother
Morrison is progressing satisfactorily, and that he extends his greetings
and good wishes to the Brethren, and, the Good Lord willing, we hopefully look forward to his presence at the next Annual Communication. We
know that our Brethren of this Grand Lodge join us in wishing him
Godspeed.
There have been referred to your Committee on Trial Review since the
1979 Communication seventeen Trial Records of which five are Petitions
for Restoration.

pr?cedur~ was followed in each case; that the result is supported by the

TRIAL RECORDS No. 1993, 2139, AND 2113
Your Committee has considered Petitions for Restoration in Trial Records 1993 a former member of Concord Lodge No. 117 and 2139, a
former m~mber of Rosemead Lodge No. 702. We believe that membership
.
in our Fraternity, once obtained should be jealously guarded.
Once membership is lost by some act of un-Masonic conduct, restoration
to the rights and privileges in Freemasonry should be granted only upon
clear and convincing evidence of atonement and rehabilitation.
In Trial Records 1993 and 2139 your Committee does not believe that
sufficient evidence of such atonement and rehabilitation has been presented.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the Petitions for Restoration in Trial Records No.
1993 and 2139 be denied.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2101
The petitioner, a former member of Temescal Lodge No. 314, was
expelled by Grand Lodge in 1977 after a confession by the petitioner to
a charge of Penal Code 647a, child molestation. After completion of
probation he petitioned for restoration to all privileges as a Master Mason .
While his recommendors are not to be ignored, and the Trial Review
Committee has given serious consideration to their statements, the nature
of the offense and the very recent release from probation warrant a
disapproval of this petition at the present time. After a period of unsupervised return to society, such a petition could again be considered.
Be it therefore RESOLVED, that the petition for restoration in Trial
Record No. 2101 be denied.
TRIAL RECORD No. 2136
The petitioner, a former member of Bell Lodge No. 483, was expelled
by Grand Lodge in 1979 for un-Masonic conduct arising from a conviction
of receiving stolen property.
The petitioner applied to Bell Lodge for restoration and upon secret
ballot, the 38 members present voted 22 "No," 7 "Yes" with 9 abstensions.
The petitioner has submitted no evidence of rehabilitation other than a
vigorous assertion of innocence.
Your Committee can find no reasonable basis to grant restoration and
in view of the failure of petitioner's Lodge to recommend restoration,
your Committee cannot justify approval of this petition.
Your Committee offers the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, the petition for restoration in Trial Record No. 2136 be
•
denied.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1283
In this case a former member of Sanger Lodge No. 316, petitions for
restoration. The Lodge expelled him effective in 1952, for un-Masonic
conduct, based on a sex offense.
Section 3514 of the California Masonic Code states in part: " .. . Restoration of a suspended or expelled Mason who has moved beyond the
jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge will be denied unless satisfactory evidence
is furnished by the action of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he at the
time resides, duly certified, that the applicant is worthy, and that his
standing and character are such as would entitle him to affiliation in such
Lodge." The obvious purpose of this require~e!lt is ,to furni~~ t~ Grand
Lodge sufficient acceptable evidence of a petitioners reha?ihtation :ind
his present reputation in his community. The petitioner in this case .resides
beyond the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, but he does not furmsh any
evidence of action by the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he now resides.
Your Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the petition for restoration in Trial Record 1283 be
denied.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2141
This trial record involves a member of Charity Lodge No. 362, the
charge against the Brother being one of un-Masonic conduct, that the
Brother had been arrested and charged with the receiving and concealing
?f stolen pr~perty. The accuse.d rendered a plea of guilty to that charge
m the Supenor Court proceedmg; however, the Masonic trial resulted in
a verdict of not guilty by majority verdict of the trial commissioners.
T~is Com~ittee finds that the charges, as brought, were not properly
specific n?r, m nature, appropriate as a trial basis. Though it seems likely
that the mtent of the charges was proper, they speak to an accusation
rather than actionable conduct.
The Committee further finds that the trial procedure lacked the control
and precision necessary to protect the interests of all involved. It appears
that the absence of documentation, despite its availability, confused the
participants and clouded the issues, a situation little relieved within our
Committee. The charges are serious, if true; therefore, we believe that

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this matter deserves, in the best interests of Masonry and the accused,
further attention after amended and more specific charges are filed.
Your Committee submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the findings and penalty in Trial Record No. 2141 be
reversed and the matter remanded to Charity Lodge No. 362 with instructions to file amended charges specifying with clearness and precision the
offense complained of, pursuant to Section 3328 C.M.C., and that new
trial proceedings be thereafter had.

indicated that the trial commissioner making them would more properly
have disqualified himself.
The trial commissioners found the accused not guilty on the specification
and on the charge, although the record shows the specification and the
charge to be true beyond any reasonable doubt.
Since there is no reasonable doubt of the accused's guilt, since the
offense of receiving or possessing stolen property is by definition a crime
of moral turpitude, and since there was here the gross violation of Masonic
Jaw as set out in Section 3503 of the California Masonic Code, your
Committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the determination of the trial commission be reversed, the accused found guilty of both the charge and the specification,
and the penalty fixed at expulsion.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2151
In this case a member of Westminster-Fairview Lodge No. 629 was
charged with un-Masonic conduct, the specifications being that on or
about October 17, 1978, he committed the misdemeanor offense of violating California Penal Code Section 647(a), annoying and molesting a
child.
Upon trial by commission the member was found guilty of un-Masonic
conduct and a penalty of suspension imposed.
The member had been previously convicted in criminal court and
granted probation, at the favorable completion of which he had petitioned
and was granted an order dismissing the criminal charge and expunging
the record. Such dismissal and expungement does not prevent use of this
record in a Masonic trial since expungement does not alter the facts. All
this was in evidence before the commission at the Masonic trial, together
with the testimony of the investigating police officer and a witness who
testified for the member.
Trial procedures appear to have been in order. The accused was present
and represented by counsel, although it appears from the record he did
not testify. The evidence was sufficient and the finding of guilty should be
affirmed.
However, this Committee feels that an offense of this kind is such a
serious violation of moral law as to merit a greater penalty than suspension. It therefore recommends the penalty be increased to expulsion.
Your Committee therefore offers the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty of un-Masonic conduct be affirmed, and that the penalty be raised to expulsion.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

CONDITION OF LODGES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Brethren, it is my pleasure and duty to submit the following report in
compliance with C.M.C. Section 1114-4th.

The Inspectors' annual reports to the Grand Lecturer show very little
change from last year's reports. Approximately 400 of the Lodges are
having difficulty keeping a full line of officers. There are more Lodges
with one or more Past Masters in the progressive line than last year. One
interesting fact is noted in this year's report regarding Past Masters as
o~cer~ , and that is in f~r more instances than in the past year they are
filhng m for one year, with new Brothers then entering the line and being
assisted by this same Past Master.
One of_the prevalent comm~nts made by the Inspectors regarding
Lodges with officer shortages, is that there continues to be a lack of
interest in learning the ritual necessary to progress through the line. The
time involved is also of concern to many of the prospective officers. To
alleviate this problem it is felt the most effective program is one of
continued candidate education. It must be exactly that---<:ontinued. The
fine program presented by the then Grand Lecturer, the Very Worshipful
Donald G. Campbell, and adopted at the 1962 Annual Communication
is a good example of what can occur by not giving continuing guidance t~
an e~cellent program. The Candidate's Handbook is now being used by
relatively few of the Lodges. Now we have an additional program for
can~i~ates. It ~ommences with educational material presented prior to
rece1vmg the Fust Degree and then continuing on prior to, and following
each of the degrees. This is additional material to be presented and is not
to be a replacement for the Candidate's Handbook, but to add further
light for the candidate. These are both excellent programs and have the
full support of the Ritual Committee. Brethren, it is up to you to make
them both succe~sful. I believe if they are used to their fullest potential,
this problem of interest in your Lodges can be reversed, and as a result
the~e. will be many new Brothers interested in serving their Lodges. In
add1~1on, my Brethren, as of 8:00 A.M. this morning, another program
was implemented known as the Wardens' Workshop. This will give further
help to the Lodges for continued interest.
On the positive side of the reports on the condition of Lodges, there
are almost three hundred Lodges wbo are showing a great interest in
participation by both officers and members. They are having many events
of interest to both members and non-members. Most of these Lodges
have an outstanding Educational Committee directing their efforts to new
members.
Another interesting point contained in the reports is that very few of
the Lodges are having serious financial problems.

RECOMMEN DATION BY THE GRAND LECTURER

As a result of the heretofore mentioned Schools, meetings and conferences, and the Inspectors' reports covering the Lodg~s of this Jurisdiction,
it is the unanimous opinion of the Ritual Committee that the Grand ·
Lecturer recommend a modification for the First Degree Lecture. The
recommendation is as follows: that the portion of the Lecture appertaining
to the form, supports, covering, furniture, ornaments, lights and jew~ls of
a Lodge, how it is situated and to whom dedicated become an opt1on~l .
portion of the First Degree Lecture. This part of ~he ~ecture wo~ld remam
in the Monitor, being enclosed in brackets showmg it to be opt10n~l. The
candidate would be able to study this section of the Lecture, as with the
hieroglyphical emblems in the Third Degree Lect~re. Th_is, my Brethren,
is not a change but is a return to what was requued pnor to 1957. The
present form of the First Degree L~cture was adopted in that year.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICAT IONS

. Reports made to the Grand Lecturer show that the change in our law
m 1979 regarding physical qualification has not been a problem. The one
result of this change brought out that some of the Lodges had misinterpreted our laws as contained in the CMC prior to 1979. This was in respect
to some Lodges who had Entered Apprentices and/or Fellowcrafts with

physical defects which occurred after receiving their degree or degrees

permission to proceed with the degree wor~ for the.se c~ndidat~s. ~hus a
twofold benefit was received from the physical quahficat1on leg1slat1on.
1980-81 BUDGET

The past year has not shown any leveling off in the costs involved in
the operation of this Grand Lodge and in particular for the Ritual ~om­
mittee. As a result of the increased costs for Conferences, Semmars,
Schools and the Annual Communication it is necessary to request a budget
of seventy thousand five hundred dollars ($70,500) for 1980-81.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, a charitable
corporation organized under the laws of the State of California, respectfully presents its eighty-eighth annual report on the Masonic Homes of
California for the fiscal year July 1, 1979 through June 30, 1980.
ORGANIZAT ION OF THE BOARD

The Board of Trustees met in San Francisco, California, on October
11, 1979, for the purpose of organization. The election of H. Douglas
Lemon (699), Deputy Grand Master; Robert 0. West (26), Senior Grand
Warden; and Harry L. Maynard (214), Junior Grand Warden, was formally
reported to the Board and, pursuant to the provisions of the California
Masonic Code, they were elected members of the Board. In addition to
the Grand Lodge Officers, the Board was composed of the following
Trustees for terms as of the close of the Annual Communication of Grand
