MASONRY'S INVOLVEMENT IN VOLUNTEER SCHOOL PROGRAMS
The Public Schools Committee and the Grand Lodge of California
cooperated with the Los Angeles School Department in the continuation
of the DOVES (dedicated older volunteers in educational service) program which expanded greatly during the year. We mailed a letter from
our Grand Master to the 27 ,000 Masons living in the Los Angeles School
District area urging them or people they know to contact the DOVES
office offering their services as volunteers. With the hopeful expansion of
our Committee, we will be able to expand Masonry's involvement in
Public School volunteer programs in the future.
SALUTE To PUBLIC EDUCATION BREAKFAST
Your Public Schools Committee highly commends Most Worshipful
Vernon L. Gordon for his innovative approach to the Thursday Morning
Breakfast. To salute the educators of our school systems at the head table
and to have an outstanding speaker in the person of Dr. William S.
Benowsky, President of the University of Oklahoma, is most appropriate.
CONCLUSION
Concern was expressed this past year that we as Masons and also as
individuals do not and cannot condone some of the things that are being
done in our local schools, and that we must be careful not to let the
general public be of the opinion that we support all the actions and
programs of our local school districts. What we do support is the concept
of PUBLIC EDUCATION. The Public Schools poster and other materials
say "SUPPORT PUBLIC EDUCATION" to help bring this important
point into focus.
Deep concern is still felt by the Public Schools Committee of Grand
Lodge that too many Lodges, particularly in the metropolitan areas,
consider that they have accomplished their Masonic duty and responsibility by participating in a large joint effort with other Lodges and/or Districts
in a Public Schools Week Observance. The Committee congratulates these
Lodges in their joint efforts and certainly encourages their continuance.
However, each Lodge should be aware that there are numerous April and
year round projects for individual Lodge participation. The Committee
encourages each Lodge to have a "project of their own." Many ideas and
suggestions are contained in the green pages of the Lodge Manual. The

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON INSURANCE STUDY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the 130th Annual Communica tion a resolution was adopted by 5/6
affirmative vote which mandated the study of a self-insurance program for
the Masonic Temple Associations within this Jurisdiction. That resolution
read in part as follows:
". . . we move that the new Grand Master appoint a new Committee
to study the formation of a consortium of Constituent Temples, outside
of Grand Lodge, for the purpose of combining forces against catastrophic losses, and perhaps other desirable purposes . . . "
On April 22, 1980, the Grand Master appointed the undersigned to
serve on this Committee whose report follows:
I. SURVEY OF PRESENT INSURANC E COVERAG E AND LOSS
EXPERIEN CE.
At the Committee's organization al meeting, the members of the Committee concluded that a self-insurance program for the Masonic Temple

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

197

Associations within the States of California and Hawaii is legally possible
and would not jeopardize our tax-exempt status if the program is properly
structured. The Committee therefore determined that it should study
whether a self-insurance program would reduce insurance costs for the
participants , and, if thus shown to be economically feasible, what type of
self-insurance program would be most appropriate for Masonic Temple
Associations . The Committee retained Mr. Clarence R. Atwood, of Atwood & Co., Consulting Actuaries, to determine whether there would be
any savings from the formation of a self-insurance program and what the
magnitude of those savings would be. Mr. Atwood is a Fellow of the
Casualty Actuarial Society and a Member of the American Academy of
Actuaries. He is a former Deputy Insurance Commission er and Casualty
Actuary for the State of California and has seventeen years experience as
an actuary.
At the Committee's initial meeting with Mr. Atwood, he requested
certain information regarding the current insurance coverage of the Masonic Temple Associations in this Jurisdiction. At the request of the Committee, the Grand Master wrote all Masters on July 3, 1980, requesting
the following. If the addressed Lodge owned or had an interest in a
Masonic Temple, it was requested to send to the Committee a photocopy
of the page or pages on the insurance policies on that building which
disclosed the type of coverage, policy limit and premiums. Whether or not
the addressed Lodge owned or had an interest in a Masonic Temple, it
was requested to send copies of pages indicating type of coverage, period
of coverage, policy limit and premiums for any other policies of insurance
paid for by the Lodge (over and above the coverage furnished by the
Grand Lodge blanket policy) or by a related Masonic Temple Association.
Finally, a "RecQrd of Loss" was enclosed, to be completed and returned,
indicating whether there had been any losses for which insurance reimbursement had been requested during the last five years.
Of the approximate ly 395 Temple Associations in this Jurisdiction, 176
responded in sufficient detail to be used in the study. It was the opinion
of the actuary that the 176 responses were sufficient in number to extend
the conclusions indicated by those responses to all 395 Masonic Temple
Associations . Accordingly, based upon the responses from these 176
Lodges, Mr. Atwood computed by extrapolatio n the annual premiums
paid on insurance by all the Masonic Temple Associations in this Jurisdiction. Additionally, based upon the responses to the survey as well as
estimated average loss ratios for property holdings such as ours, as developed by the insurance industry, Mr. Atwood computed the average
annual losses from risks covered by insurance for all Masonic Temple
Associations. The insurance disclosed in the survey as carried by the
Masonic Temple Associations typically covered the following risks:
Fire
Comprehens ive Public Liability
Medical Payments
Worker's Compensati on
Employer's Liability

199

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Mr. Atwood advised the Committee that the savings from a self-insurance program would increase as more entities under the control of the
Grand Lodge joined the program. The Committee therefore requested
and received from the Grand Secretary's office premium information on
insurance coverage furnished by the Grand Lodge blanket policy. This
policy contains the following coverages:
Comprehensive Public Liability
Medical Payments
Fidelity
Money and Securities
Depositor's Forgery
Paraphernalia
Worker's Compensation
This insurance is billed to the Grand Lodge and is paid for by each
individual Lodge through the per capita tax. This blanket policy covers
the insurance risks of each individual Masonic Lodge. It is in addition to
the risks borne by the separate Masonic Temple Associations which may
own the facilities in which the Lodges meet.
The Committee also requested and received from the Grand Secretary's
office premium information on insurance carried by the Grand Lodge on
behalf of itself as well as on behalf of the following entities under the
control of the Grand Lodge:
Masonic Homes of California
California Masonic Memorial Temple
The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund
California Masonic Retirement Plan
Masonic Service Bureaus
California Masonic Foundation
All of the above information was used by the actuary in the preparation
of his report which was presented to the Committee on September 22,
1980.

II . CONCLUSIONS OF THE ACTUARY.
The survey enabled the actuary to study two separate and distinct
problems. In addition to determining whether some type of self-insurance
program was economically feasible, the survey permitted the actuary to
estimate the adequacy of the present fire and other property loss insurance
coverage carried by the local Masonic Temple Associations.
A. Adequacy of Fire and Other Property Loss Insurance Carried by
Masonic Temple Associations.
The survey indicated that many Masonic Temple Associations are
grossly underinsured with respect to their fire and other property loss
insurance coverage. These Temple Associations insured their buildings
and other improvements at maximum values considerably below the estimated replacement cost of these improvements. This could cause grave
financial problems for an underinsured Temple Association should there

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

cost of insurance, smaller Lodges with older membersh ips find it difficult
to pay ·for any insurance other than for casualty losses. As an alternative ,
we would suggest that these Lodges consider a property loss policy with
an increased deductible. A deductible of $1,000 to $10,000 greatly reduces
the premium costs but insures against a catastroph ic loss. The present
resources of the Lodge or Temple Association may be able to absorb small
losses but probably would not sustain the entire destructio n of their building.

The only responsibility of the trustees of the insurance ~rust ~~uld be

B. Econoic Feasibility of a Self-Insurance Program
Based upon the Committe e's survey, the actuary has determine d that a
self-insurance program would provide substantial savings for all participants and would therefore be economically feasible. In reaching his conclusions, the actuary has assumed that this program would be comprised
of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California, the Masonic Homes of
California , the California Masonic Memorial Temple, other entities of the
Grand Lodge whose insurance is administered through the Grand Lodge,
including the blanket policy covering the individual Lodges, as well as
such of the Masonic Temple Associations in the Jurisdiction as elect to
participate in the program.
(1) Insurance Trust
The first step in the self-insurance program would be formation of an
insurance trust. Based upon competitive bidding, the trust would secure
one or more master policies covering the insurable risks of the participants. Under California law, there must be at least two master policies:
one covering workmen's compensa tion insurance separate from one covering other risks. Although there would be one set of master policies,
certificates of insurance would be issued to each participan t. This is very
similar to an employer' s master group insurance policy with certificates of
insurance issued to each employee insured under the policy. The valuation
of the property to be insured under each certificate as well as the deductible in case of loss would vary depending upon the final decision of the
participan t after considering appraisals which the participan t would be
encourage d to obtain on its buildings. The administra tion of the insurance
program would be conducted entirely by the insurance company or companies writing the master policies. The insurance company or companies
successfully bidding on the master policies would:
(a) rate, quote and issue all certificates as well as the master policies,
(b) collect all premiums ,
(c) manage all claims,
(d) provide an appraisal program to establish proper values,
(e) pay for a separate statistical program which would include a
quarterly compilation and analysis of the experience for review by the
insurance trust, and
(f) provide a safety engineering service to randomly inspect and
encourage Masonic Temple Association's compliance with applicable fire,
safety and health ordinance s and regulations.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

exchange economically feasible, it would be necessary for the annual
premiums to be at least $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 a year.

(f) The Grand Lodge advance to the Committee such funds as are
necessary to continue this study; provided that these advances shall be
returned to the Grand Lodge as soon as possible from monies collected
by the trust from participants, should such trust eventually be established.
(g) The trustees of any insurance trust subsequently approved by
the Grand Lodge should periodically review whether the amount of premiums and insurance risks administered by the trust justifies the formation
of an inter-insurance exchange.
Recommendation 2. The Committee, its successor or another established Committee of the Grand Lodge should commence and administer
an appraisal program to assist the Masonic Temple Associations of this

However, the ultimate responsibility for that appraisal must rest with the
individual Masonic Temple Association. Each Masonic Temple Association should be encouraged to obtain independently a professional appraisal
of its property.

III. RECOMMENENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE.
Based upon the September 22nd report of the actuary as well as its
review .by the Committee and the Committee's separate deliberations, the
Committee recommends the following:
Recommendation 1. Because the actuarial report indicates substantial
savings for the participants in an insurance trust, the Committee recommends that it, or a successor Committee, in the discretion of the incoming
Grand Master, continue this study and prepare a proposal for the formation of such an insurance trust, if feasible, for consideration at the 132nd
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, to be held in October, 1981.
This trust should be drafted to provide by means of competitive bid master
insurance policies covering the insurance risks of all entities which pres~ntly secur~ their insurance through the Grand Lodge as well as the
i~~uranc~ nsk.s of those Masonic Temple Associations which wish to participate m this program. The Committee further recommends that the
following limitations be strictly observed in order to protect this Grand
Lodge and all entities which participate in this program:
(a) I!' order t.h~t this Grand Lodge will incur no liability by reason
of the creation of this insurance trust, other than for premiums for insurance coverage which it obtains through the trust, the insurance trust must
be a separately incorporated entity similar to the California Masonic
Memorial Temple.
(b) Although it is the Committee's opinion that the formation and
administrat.ion of a~ insurance trust will not affect our tax-exempt status,
the Committee or its successor must establish through a private ruling
from the Internal Revenue Service, written opinion of tax counsel or
otherwise, that the particular Articles of Incorporation prepared for the
proposed insurance trust, its by-laws, and the procedures to administer
the trust will not in any way affect the tax-exempt status of the Grand
Lodge or any of its subordinate bodies.
.
(c) No certificate of insurance under any master policy may be
wnt~en for any proposed participant until the insurance regulatory authonty of the state under whose jurisdiction such participant exists has
approved participation in the insurance trust.
(d) Participation in the program should initially be limited to the
Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes of California, California Masonic Memorial Temple, The Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, California Masonic
Retirement Plan, Masonic Service Bureaus, and California Masonic Foun?ation and such of the. Masonic Temple Associations as wish to participate
m the program; provided, however, that the trust should not prohibit
other Masonic affiliated bodies from participation should this be deemed
desirable after the successful establishment and operation of such a trust.
(e) The insurance trust should not be formed unless 130 (which is
approximately one-third) of the Masonic Temple Associations in this Jurisdiction indicate their willingness to participate in the program.

RESOLVED, that the incoming Grand Master shall see to the implementation of Recommendations 1 and 2 of the Report of the Special
Committee on Insurance Study presented at this 131st Annual Communication.

REPORT OF THE FELLOWSHIP NIGHT
SPEAKERS PANEL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The members of the Fellowship Night Speakers Panel are pleased to
present the following report of activities for the 1979-1980 Grand Lodge
year.
Many men live their entire lives through and never learn they must ask
for admission to the world's oldest and most purposeful Fraternity-Freemasonry. They do not realize that they cannot be invited to join.
Many persons, including women, wonder what Freemasonry is, what it
stands for-its place in contemporary society.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The purpose of this Panel is to answer that wonderment through talks
about Freemasonry given within the friendly confines of neighborhood
Lodges and inviting interested non-Masons and women to attend.
After dinner, the invited guests along with their Masonic friends learn
something about Masonic history, Grand Lodge, Constituent Lodges,
membership requirements, Masonic secrecy, Freemasonry and religion,
Masonic tenets, what Masonry is--and what it isn't, etc. Guests are invited
to ask questions and their questions are answered.
The enthusiasm of participating Lodges has been outstanding, and we
refer all Worshipful Masters to those Lodges for their endorsement of the
program.

guest speakers: Kermit A. Jacobson, P.G.M., Edward E. Seagle, C. Clifford Geddes, Leo B. Mark, Robert L. Sorensen.

REPORT OF
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT COMMITTE E
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Lodge Resources Development Committee has held itself in readiness and has carried out assignments in two separate fields.
1. The original plan of the Committee continues as an important function in that the Committee is available for consultation with a subordinate
Lodge which feels that outside assistance is needed. The procedure is for
such a Lodge to make known its needs to the Grand Master, and if the
Grand Master feels that a visit by members of the LRD Committee would
be beneficial, he requests that Committee schedule the event.
The Chairmap then appoints a Sub-committee and carries on correspondence, selecting the date when the Sub-committee can appear and
arranging with those who can make the necessary appearance. Two Lodges
have availed themselves of services; one in the City of Long Beach, and
one in the City of Sacramento. In each case, the Sub-committee met with
a sizeable delegation of members of the Lodge and satisfactory progress
was made. The report circulates from the Sub-committee to the main
Committee. In the appearance at Long Beach, the Sub-committee was
joined by a number of members from the Charters Committee, so that a
joint report could be prepared. The work at Sacramento is not yet complete.
2. A new and useful plan was devised by Most Worshipful Vernon L.
Gordon, Grand Master, which has become known as the "18 Point Plan".
The name arises from the fact that he has designated 18 activities, which
he believes are beneficial to the subordinate Lodge. If at least 12 of these
18 projects are completed during the Masonic year, then the Lodge becomes eligible for a certificate of recognition to be distributed at the
Annual Communication. This idea is new to California and has been

206

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

accepted readily. It has created interest. Many of the projects suggested
have been advocated for years, but this offers a new approach to an old
problem and the Committee is much encouraged and is pleased that the
Grand Master would accept the services of the Committee in seeing that
it is carried out. It is hoped that the same plan or one similar to it will be
carried forward in the future.
Respectfully submitted,

COMMITTEE ON OLD MASONIC HALL
AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
This miniature edifice, steeped in Masonic traditions for more than 120
years, attracted a visitation by more than 1400 persons, many of whom
were non-Masons, from all over the United States, as well as from other
countries in the world.
We had visitors from Germany, England, France, Australia, Greece,
South American nations, Israel and even two persons from Russia, all of
whom signed our guest book.
For the first time since the Temple became State Historical Monument
No. 23, it was completely repainted and its old wooden floors were stained
and waxed. Man·y of the Masonic artifacts in the interior were polished
and a modern fire extinguishing system is to be installed by the State later
this year. The State is also going to install a modern air conditioning plant
on the premises.
The Temple, site of the first Masonic Home for Los Angeles Lodge No.
42 in 1859, is open on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday from 1
to 5 P.M. Only one Lodge utilizes the site for its monthly meetings,
although a number of Masonic youth organizations rent the hall for their
monthly meetings.
We look towards a busy year in the months ahead as Los Angeles
celebrates its Bicentennial. The Old Temple is located in the center of "El
Pueblo de Los Angeles," epicenter of celebration activities.
Respectfully submitted,
MATIHEW M. CODON, Chairman

GLENN H. HARMAN

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC INFORMATION AND RESPONSIBILITY

These speakers were taken from outside the Committee and provided a
most vital part of the Program.
The Masonic Information for Candidates Program of the I. & R. Committee is progressing throughout most of the Northern Californi~ a~ea.
The program is being used by many more Lodges now than at this time
last year. Many of the 1980 Senior Wardens have indicated that they would
implement this program after their probable installation as Masters of
their respective Lodges for the year 1981.
.
Lodges which have conscientiously used this program smce shortly after
its introduction into California slightly more than a year ago have been
unanimous in their enthusiastic approval of it. A number of the Masters
who introduced it into their Lodges are continuing with it as Chairmen of
their Lodges' Candidate Information Programs.
Candidates who have taken the Program have, in their observations
about it, been most enthusiastic in their approval. In several instances,
newly raised Master Masons have stated that the Masonic Light disclos~d
in the series of Candidate Information Lectures has had a large part m
causing them to become the enthusiastic Masons they are.
In Division No. I, good progress has been made during the past year,
and we may look forward to even more progress for 1981. Committeeman
Robert J. Schulte, P. M. No. 375, should be especially mentioned for his
successful efforts in contacting, and assisting the Masters in his area to
get started on the Candidates' Program, and for his additional success in
introducing a Leadership Program in the Lodges assigned to him. Other
areas have also enjoyed unusually capable assistance from our Committeemen in starting the Candidates' Programs.
The Second and Fourth Divisions, in those areas which were reasonably
close, geographieally, to the areas where the Committeemen resided, have
shown progress in the acceptance and implementation of the Candidates'
Program. Because of lack of manpower in the far northern parts of California and in the Central Valley area, progress can be improved upon
there.
The effect of Committee support in the greater San Francisco area has
been weakened somewhat by health problems, but the Committeemen
are now whole again, and our next report should show an increased
momentum there.
All reports from Committeemen indicate that when the Program has
been successfully practiced for even a short while by one or two Lodges
in an area, other Lodges note the values, and follow by starting their own
programs.
.
Overall, in the short time that this program has been applied by the
Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction, our progress has shown its value and
the obvious need to continue the ever more rapid acceptance and implementation of the Candidates' Information Program by our Constituent
Lodges becomes apparent.
We are particularly grateful for the cooperation received from the Assistant Grand Lecturers, Inspectors and the Resource speakers who helped
to make this program so meaningful.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Following the close of Grand Lodge last October a well planned program
to implement the desires and wishes of our Grand Master was instituted,
that we might bring our message to the entire membership. I can not
report that we were completely successful but much has been accomplished this past year, and we are grateful for the opportunity to have
served.
In planning the program with the Grand Master, it was his desire that
Seminar type meetings be held in each of the six Divsions of our Jurisdiction. Two in Divisions I, II and IV and three in Divisions III, V and
VI.
Our Liaison Officer, the Deputy Grand Master, was assigned to carry
our Program to the Brethren at the Grand Master's Seminars in each of
the six Divisions.
In a meeting with our Liason Officer in November your Chairman was
asked to prepare a Job Description for the Committee and the following
was prepared: "The Duties of the Masonic Information and Responsibility
Committee are two-fold:
1. To gather information pertinent to the policies and programs of the
Grand Lodge as promulgated by the Grand Master and distribute
the same to the Lodges and Brethren upon the approval of the Grand
Master.
2. To encourage and assist the Lodges, Officers and Brethren in the
perfection of their skills in the area of Education & Leadership that
they may effectually promote the Policies and Programs of the Grand
Lodge."
With our duties outlined by the Grand Master, the Committee set to
work for the year. A meeting was held for those members in the North in
November and one for those in the South in January, at which time our
duties were outlined and each member was assigned several Masonic
Districts to meet with the several Lodges assigned to them. Each of the
Committeemen performed yeoman service, meeting with the Lodge Officers at the District Officers Schools of Instruction called by the Inspectors
and with the individual Lodges when invited to do so. Their program
followed the Lodge System of Masonic Information for Candidates Education as well as pointing out the importance of the Monitor and the
Handbook for Candidate Coaches.
In addition to the work of the individual Committeemen, Seminars
were held in Divisions I, II, III & VI. These were held in conjunction
with the Division Inspectors & Officers Schools called by the Assistant
Grand Lecturers. Here again the Lodge System of Masonic Information
for Candidates was presented along with the other books provided by the
Grand Lodge. A Resource speaker was provided to talk on Leadership.

REPORT OF MASONIC HISTORY COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History was engaged in the following
activities during the past year:
1. The Committee continued to distribute the "Instant History" form
to the Lodges. The form is one which makes it easy for the Lodges
to simply fill in the blanks for the past year.
2. The Committee has received more pictures of Lodge Temples and
the completed "Instant History" forms.
3. The Committee has continued to receive and organize memorabilia
from the Brethren of the California Lodges. The documents are to
be deposited in the archives of the Grand Lodge.

211

The Committee answered many questions asked of it during the
last year. Of course, the Committee welcomes inquiries on the
subject from the Lodges or the Brethren.
5. The Committee explored the following areas during the past year:
a. Photographed and researched Table Mountain Lodge No. 124 of
Paradise, the other half of Masons in Paradise (Paradise Park,
Santa Cruz-home of Masons and members of Masonic associated bodies and their families).
b. Wrote the intriguing history of San Jacinto Lodge No. 338.
c. Completed work on the research of eleven Masons and their
contribution to the reform of city government in Fresno.
d. Continued the research of Masons working in the oil fields
around Bakersfield.
e. Explored the activities of Masons in pre-World War II Santa
Barbara.
f. Researched Mother Lode Masonry in the Sutter Creek area.
g. Looked into Masons and Masonry in several of the desert areas
of California.
6. Prepared photograph albums covering the following subjects:
a. Cornerstone Laying Ceremony-Charles H. Sedam Center, Masonic Home, Union City.
b. The Grand Master's Visit to the Masonic Home, Union City.
c. Dedication-Charles H. Sedam Center, Masonic Home, Union
City.
d. Mariner's Night at San Pedro-Brothers Gerald Ford and Gene
Autry received awards.
e. Most Worshipful John Robert's Travels during His Year as Grand
Master:
f. The Re-Laying of the Cornerstone of the State Capital at Sacramento.
7. The Committee Chairman in an informal, unofficial discussion with
the Librarian and Curator of the Museum of the Grand Lodge of
Pennsylvania determined that that Grand Jurisdiction would be
willing to discuss the possibility of a one year exchange of items of
Masonic historical significance between the respective Grand
Lodges. In this way, Masons of both Jurisdictions will be able to
see items which would ordinarily not be available to them. Such
memorabilia could cover the Mother Lode and Colonial periods of
history. A letter covering the details has been filed with the Assistant Grand Secretary for review at the next Grand Lodge Communication, or befor~, at the pleasure of the Grand Master.

4.

Your Masonic History Committee requests a budget in the
amount of $650 to continue its current work and engage in other
projects for the service and information for the Grand Lodge, its
Constituent Lodges and the Brethren.

REPORT OF
THE QUITMAN MASONIC TEMPLE COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Upon assuming the office of Grand Master in October 1979, the Most
Worshipful Vernon L. Gordon reappointed four of the existing members
to the Grand Lodge Quitman Temple Committee. These were William H.
Lambert (13), Chairman, Steve M. Chileski (23), Kennith Lackey (13)
and Demar Dundas (13). Martin Johnson (13) was replaced by Paul
McKee (59). Lambert again invited Robert Richier (13), not a Past Master, to attend all meetings as a special consultant.
Three Committee meetings were held during the year, with four or
more members present at all meetings. The Committee also held two
work days at the Temple.
An important accomplishment was made in early September 1979,
which was too late to be included in the report for last year. The sixty feet
of molding (or trim) around the recessed ceiling was installed. This type
of molding is no longer on the market, so the Brethren cast it from
"hydrocal," which is used for making false teeth. It was made in sixty inch
lengths, attached with lag screws, and then the joints were plastered over.
Brother Martin Johnson had gained some experience in this type of work
during construction of the I. Magnin mansion 36 years earlier.
Another important accomplishment during the year was replacing the
ceiling lights in the Tiler's room and preparation room with historical
reproductions in copper, custom made in Maine. The lights replaced were
plain porcelain sockets with a single light bulb, and they definitely did not
fit the 1870 period. Some short rips in the 74 year old carpet were mended,
some plain doorknobs were replaced with knobs of antique brass, and a
roof leak around the stovepipe was repaired. The equipment cabinet in
the closet off the preparation room was painted. A flagstaff for the 37 star
flag was acquired, but it is not quite ancient enough or sufficiently battered
to fit the Gold Rush Period. A brass adapter was made for the antique
marble flagstand, which goes well with our ancient flag.
Two Lodges made visitations to Quitman Temple prior to the date of
this report, and another visitation was expected for September 13. Lakeshore Lodge No. 551 of San Lorenzo conferred a third degree there on
March 22, and Nevada Lodge No. 13 also conferred a third degree on
August 15. Pittsburg Lodge No. 429 was planning to confer a third degree
in the Temple on September 13.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

213

In spite of the high price of gasoline, the Park Rangers at Malakoff
Diggins State Park are predicting a total of approximately 18,500 visitors
to the Park for the 1980 tourist season. Of these, close to 3,000 would
make the conducted tour, which includes Quitman Temple. A few Masons
volunteered to serve as guides or attendants on weekends and holidays.
The Temple was open for visitors on June 8, when over 3,000 people were
in the Park for the annual "Home-Coming" Celebration.
All of the construction work at the Quitman Temple is now complete.
The Temple is also completely furnished except it lacks a suitable desk
for the Secretary's station. Our Committee has been trying for over two
years to find an antique roll-top desk. There is a possibility that one might
be loaned to the Temple for an indefinite period. There are good quality
new reproductions on the market for around $1,000, but it would spoil
the effect to put a reproduction in a room full of genuine antiques. The
average price of an antique roll-top desk is now around $2,000. In our
1981 budget we are asking for this amount, so we may purchase one
outright if we don't get one on loan or find a real bargain by July 31,
1980. This would be a one time expenditure, and barring a disaster, it
should last indefinitely.
In our proposed budget for next year we have requested funds to
reimburse Masons who use their personal cars when they serve as guides
at the Quitman Temple on weekends or holidays. We budgeted for this in
1980, but only one Mason has submitted a mileage claim. The average
round trip to the Temple from the Nevada City-Gra ss Valley area is 60
miles. At 15 cents per mile this would come to $9.00 for each round trip.
If there is a Mason in the Temple every weekend and holiday, it will
require 40 round trips and the cost would be $312. However, we can't find
that many voluoteers and most of them cheerfully donate the use of their
cars. We are also asking for $50 to allow for miscellaneous maintenance
expenses. This·makes a total of $2410.
After we get the Secretary's desk, this Committee may be able to
operate for as little as $100 a year. As the Temple becomes better known
it will be having more visitations from Lodges all over Northern California.
Grand Lodge receives $25 for each visitation, so Quitman Temple may be
paying its own way in the near future.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM A. LAMBERT, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON YOUTH ORDERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
This past year your Youth Orders Committee has been very active. The
area co-chairman organization, utilizing six different areas for the State
to give local control, is working extremely well. As a result, we were able
to publish and distribute the "Putting the YOU in YOUth" brochure at
last year's Annual Communication. Each of the six areas met at least four
times last year; this gave better coverage to local problems at a reduced
cost to Grand Lodge. The Committee also met twice last year, half in the
North and half in the South, to kick off the year and to discuss the new
programs that are being developed.
This year we are introducing an award to recognize those Masons who
have given their time and service to our Masonic Affiliated youth. These
men have received little, if any, recognition from us in the past and it's
long overdue. They put in long hours of service to our youth and are away
from their families four out of five nights a week. Their examples of
unselfish service, honesty, and comradeship, to name just a few, bring our
Masonic ideals to our youth. If only three of our Masonic tenets-Brotherly Love, Relief, and Truth-were practiced in every home, how different
our newspaper headlines would read. How do we educate everyone to
practice these ideals? By starting with our youth as these men have. This
is why we are introducing an award to allow you to honor them for the
service they bring not only to our youth, but to our Masonic Fraternity as
well . The name for this award is appropriately being selected by our youth
and will be announced at this Annual Communication during the presentation of our youth. Other programs are in the works and are scheduled
to be announced later in the year.
My Brethren, our youth still desperately need your help! They are doing
their part-the Rainbow for Girls have selected the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation as their charity for the year. Job's Daughters are raising money for
a stained glass window to be installed in the Chapel at our own home at
Union City, and the International Master Councilor for DeMolay is from
our own Southern Jurisdiction. Unfortunately, we are not doing our part.
The biggest problem confronting our youth groups is the lack of adult
leadership. Our DeMolay Chapters are still being closed because of a lack
of adult Masonic leaders. In addition, some of our Temple Associations
are forcing our youth to meet outside of our Temples because of high
rents. My Brethren, we cannot expect our youth to carry the same financial
burdens as we do. Their membership is considerably smaller than ours,
twenty to thirty members with a maximum of around sixty. Please review
your Temple Association's actions regarding our youth. You may be surprised.
The accomplishments that have been made by our Committee this past
year, would not have been possible without the effort of some of our key
people. Again this year, Brother Howard Spiegel, Co-Chairman of Area
VI, San Diego, has been a spark plug for our Committee. He has introduced new programs on the local level as well, to give the Masters and

215

Inspectors a chance to meet some of the adult youth leaders and to listen
and begin to understand some of their problems.
Brother George Dress, Co-Chairman of Area I, San Francisco, has been
a real support to the Committee. He has also introduced new innovations
to his area and is responsible for the location and set up of the Youth
Orders booth. Brother Bob Watkins, Co-Chairman of Area II, Sacramento, has been a real help in getting our new programs sta~ted with
recommendations for certificates and plaque layouts. These are JUSt a few
of our many hard working Committeemen. Thanks, Brethren, for all of
.
.
your efforts.
It is with a real sense of loss to the Committee that I note the passmg
of Brother Norm Shanks, Co-Chairman of Area V, Santa Ana, Orange
County. Brother Shanks was very active with the Committee .and was
responsible in a large part for the format of the program we are introducing. We will miss him greatly.
We want to express our thanks to Brother Bob Klinger and his office
staff without whose help our programs would have died a premature
death.
Remember, my Brethren, this Youth Orders Committee is yours. Please
make use of it. Let's put the YOU in YOUth!
Respectfully submitted,
DAVID H. FARLEE, Chairman

REPORT OF REVIEW OF PROCEEDINGS COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the Masonic Year, your Committee reviewed the proceedings of
23 Grand Jurisdictions and one Research Lodge, including 8 Foreign
Bodies.
In general, the condition of Masonry in the United States, the Englishspeaking nations, Japan and the Philippines, is healthy, in spite of an
overall decline in membership.
Of the 21 Grand Jurisdictions which reported membership statistics,
only 3 showed a gain in membership, those being Arizona, Florida and
South Carolina. Of these 21, with a total membership of 864,700, there
was a membership loss of 10,090, or 1.17%. Of the three other jurisdictions, Mexico showed a 5% loss, with no numbers, and the Philippines
showed strength.
South Carolina, with a net gain of 487 in a membership of 74,924, was
distinguished by a vital and interesting Masonic year. The "Travelling
Bible" was returned to Grand Lodge after a 10 year journey, it having
been placed on the altar of each Lodge in numerical succession by the
officers of the preceeding Lodge. South Carolina also had a program of
open-air meetings, well received by the Craft.
New Jersey was distinguished by the greatest loss in 1978, with a 2177
loss out of 74,709 members. New Jersey also expelled a Past Grand Master
on 15 counts, including embezzeling $18,000 of Grand Lodge funds.
Missouri, with an 1847 member loss out of 97 ,322 in 1978, was a close
second. 136 Lodges out of 671 did not raise a candidate in 1978. 1467
Master Masons were suspended for N.P.D.
Arizona, although it reported a 127 member gain in its 16,070 membership, was the only jurisdiction to report an unhealthy financial condition.
All the above compare to our Grand Lodge for 1979 as follows: Out of
a membership of 202,027, California suffered a net loss of 3,963, or
1.96%, somewhat above the average loss of the 21 Grand Jurisdictions

Respectfully submitted,
HERBERT B. BLANKS, Chairman

Section 23---"The person who undertakes to indemnify another by insurance is the insurer and the person indemnified is the insured."
Section 700---"A person shall not transact any class of insurance business
in this state without first being admitted for such class. Such admission
is secured by procuring a certificate of authority from the Commissioner.

REPORT OF INSURANCE COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The function of your Special Committee on Insurance is to assist the
Grand _Master and Grand Secretary on such matters involving insurance
protection of t_he property and exposure to financial risk of Grand Lodge
and the Constituent Lodges and the responsibilities of their Officers.
Our Gra!ld Master h~s r~que~ted our Committee to study and report
on Resolution No. 1 which 1s bemg submitted at our 131st Annual Communication, entitled " Cooperative Non-Profit Insurance Scheme."
This matter has come before this body in 1977, 1978 and last year and
each year your Insurance Committee has given serious study to the question. After several conferences with the attorneys for the Insurance Commissione~ for the State of California, we determined it would be possible
to orgamze a Self Insured Non-Profit Insurance Program for Constituent
Lodges and Temple Associations under Grand Lodge jurisdiction, but in
order to do this, we would have to comply with the law.
The law under the California Insurance Code describes "insurance" as
follows:
Section 22-"lnsurance is a contract whereby one undertakes to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from a contingent
or unknown event."

Under the proposed Resolution No. 1, a cooperative scheme as suggested therein would constitute transaction of insurance, because the premiums or assessments to the various Temples participating would have to
pay for any loss sustained by one or more member of the group and such
a plan would have to comply with Section 700.
However, the law would not apply to an individual or a legal entity
willing to assume his or its own risk and self insure. As suggested by the
attorney for the Insurance Commissioner a legal entity for a self insurance
plan for Temple Associations would require creating a separate corporation or holding company for holding title to Temple properties under
which each Temple Association would transfer title and hold stock, in
which case the corporation could self insure and assess each Temple
Association, set up reserves for losses or secure coverage in the open
insurance market at possibly better negotiated rates. The possibility of
this occurring is not very bright.
The alternative to a self insurance program as suggested by the attorney
for the Insurance Commissioner is to organize a reciprocal insurance
company as required by Section 700 of the Code which would require at
least $900,000 ba5ic for capital and surplus and a considerable amount for
organization. The prospect of securing this amount of money from Grand
Lodge or the Temple Associations is not very bright.
Concerning the second part of Resolution No. 1 for Grand Lodge to
rebate 50% of insurance premiums applying to Temple Association's owning real property, which no doubt will be referred to the Finance Committee, we call attention to data developed by our Insurance Committee
when we conducted a survey two years ago when 276 Temple Associations
out of 426 reported a total of $246,000 paid annually for fire insurance or
physical damage to Temple properties.
If Grand Lodge is expected to pay 50% of this amount, the money will
have to come from the per capita assessment to each Lodge which will
mean that those Lodges who do not own any real property will be paying
a part of the premium for the Temple Associations that do, which is not
fair.
Therefore, this Committee recommends that the Resolution be rejected
and the entire matter consigned to innocuous desuetude.
At the 130th session of Grand Lodge last year, Resolution No. 6, on
the same subject of self insurance, was withdrawn and a substitute Resolution was presented authorizing the Grand Master to appoint a Committee to "study the formation of a consortium of Constituent Temples for

o!her_ desuable purposes" to be composed of Temple officers experiencing

In compliance with this authorization, the Grand Master circularized all

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Grand Lodge Library and Museum Committee has the pleasure to
submit the following annual report for the year July 1, 1979 through June
30, 1980.
The following is a resume of our activities:
Books and Studies Loaned .................... .................... .......... 599

We are pleased to call attention to the increase in books loaned due to
new reader interest plus new book titles. Noteworthy among the donors:
Br~ther John Bellman-33 Volumes of Egyptology, Mythology Esoterica.

Among our book purchases were a 12 volume set of the Old Testament
and Torah, studies in the Jewish tradition. A 12 volume set of the Interpreters Bible in the Protestant tradition. In addition, 24 cassette tapes
were acquired from the Oregon Research Lodge; talks by eminent Masonic scholars on a variety of subjects, i.e. Harry Carr---600 Years of Craft
Ritual; Alex Horne-Source of Masonic Symbolism; Eugene Hopp--History of Prince Hall Masonry.
Several of the new books purchased are of especial interest to Masons
and Masonic scholars and are avialable for loan. In addition, a number of
books were purchased dealing with Lodge and officer aids, speeches,
prayers, Lodge Bulletin space fillers, etc.
Research was undertaken for the California Historical Society, studies
for two Masonic authors and Masonic family roots for four individuals.
Assistance was furnished to Miss Lynn Roberts of the University of
California and Mr. Tony Fels of Stanford University, doctoral candidates
studying and writing on the Masonic Fraternity.
Work of reorganization in the Library is progressing favorably, i.e.,
updating the file;;, preparing and assembling new cards for our file case,
preparation of a new Library manual for use by the staff as well as
preparation of a more convenient means for reserving books and identifying overdue books.

COMMITTEE TO STUDY
TEMPLE INSURANCE MATTERS
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the Report of the Special
Committee on Insurance Study has been referred, reports as follows:
This Committee is seriously concerned with the legal effect of an insurance trust or an inter-insurance exchange upon the tax exempt status
of this Grand Lodge and its tax exempt entities. We are equally concerned
with the possibility of legal liability jeopardizing the assets and resources

226

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

227

of this Grand Lodge in the event of catastrophic loss for which the capitalization of the trust or inter-insurance exchange is inadequate. Moreover,
the validity of such a program in relation to Section 2300 of the California
Masonic Code governing the necessity of Lodges to control their own
funds, is still an unanswered question. However, such matters are not now
before this Committee, as no legislation is involved in the motion to adopt
the Special Committee Report.
A strict reading of Recommendation No. 1 of the Committee requires
the preparation of a proposal for the formation of an insurance trust, or
inter-insurance exchange whether or not the study to be made concluded
that it is feasible.
The Chairman of the Committee stated that this was not the intent of
the Committee and has agreed to amend Recommendation 1 by inserting
the words "if feasible" after the words "study" in line 5 so that it will read,
in part, the" ... Grand Master, continue this study and if feasible, prepare
a proposal for the formation" etc.
For this reason, and solely to bring the matter before you, we move the
adoption of the Report of the Special Committee on Insurance Study, as
amended.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 8, held over from 1979 Communication, would permit
Decisions and Recommendations of the Grand Master which have the
effect of changing our law to be voted upon directly without requiring a
motion and five-sixths vote to enable such Decision or Recommendation
to be brought before the delegates for vote. The double vote required
under present law is often confusing to the delegates and serves no useful
purpose.
Prior to voting, the Brethren of Grand Lodge will have already heard
the Grand Master's Message, which includes any decisions or recommendations which would have the effect of changing our law. Proceeding
directly to vote on a decision or recommendation would seem to be the
next proper and understandable step.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "YES"
vote.
Adopted--213 vote.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS COMMITTEE- SIZE
(1979 Resolution No. 10)
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Referred to 1979 Report (See 1979 Proceedings, page 243)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Holdover Resolution No. 10 proposes to increase the size of the Public
Schools Committee to a maximum of 40 members.
For a number of years there has been a decline both in the number of
Lodges in this Jurisdiction and in the overall membership of the Lodges.
One result of that decline has been a reduction in the size of the base for
per capita taxation at the same time that there has been a general and
sizeable increase in expense due to inflation. Though a "whereas" clause
in the original resolution stated that there was no anticipated increase in
the budgeted expenses over the year in which the resolution had been
presented, it is only realistic to assume that an increase of one-third in the
size of a committee eventually will produce an increase in expenses-which increase must then be included in the Annual Budget of the Grand
Lodge and also included in the per capita tax. This is a good and sufficient
reason in and of itself for the Grand Lodge at this time to reject increases
in the size of any Committee.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes does not believe that
it is necessary for the Public Schools Committee to attempt individual
contact by its members with every Lodge in the Jurisdiction to accomplish

"The Committee on Public Schools shall develop and promote methods
of increasing interest in and support for the public schools among the
Craft and the public."
The key words here are "develop and promote methods of increasing
interest and support."
For many years that Committee has devoted itself to encouraging visitations to Public Schools during a period determined by the Grand Master
for an annual observance. But times change and so do problems, thus
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes encourages the Committee on Public Schools to address itself to today's needs. To do so, we
believe, requires intensified effort to develop and promote-to lead and
not merely to follow. We also believe that the constitutional size of the
Committee on Public Schools is adequate to accomplish this purpose.
Therefore, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "NO" vote.
The Committee on Public Schools:
The Committee on Public Schools reports on Holdover Resolution
Number 10 as follows:
As last year when the resolution was originally balloted upon, the Public
Schools Committee again unanimously recommends a "YES" vote.
The resolution was submitted to the 1979 Grand Lodge Communication
with the encouragement and assistance of members of the Policy and
General Purposes Committee. This resolution received a recommendation
for a "YES" vote from Policy and General Purposes, and you Brethren
responded with over 1600 "YES" votes - just 82 votes short of the
necessary five-sixths majority to effect adoption. Consequently, the resolution is a holdover to this present Grand Lodge Communication.
However, to the utter dismay and astonishment of your Public Schools
Committee, the Committee on Policy and General Purposes is reversing
their recommendation in a great measure because of the results of the
Grand Lodge Organizational study that was reported upon yesterday. The
study reported that committees of other Jurisdictions are generally smaller
than our Public Schools Committee. However, the study goes on to say
on page 24 that the smaller sizes of Committees in other Jurisdictions
"might not be efficient for California because of size and distance." The
Commission report goes on to say on page 25 that "Committee size should
be that which is judged to be appropriate to the assigned responsibility of
each Committee." The ASSIGNED RESPONSIBILITIES of your Public
Schools Committee necessitate the increase in allowable membership to
properly perform its function as laid down in Section 1212 of our Masonic
Code. This resolution merely authorizes 40 members and does not mandate same. No budgetary increase is anticipated as a result of adopting

This occurs in the third section of the Third Degree material, which
furnishes some details of the building of King Solomon's Temple, toward
the end of which it is said that
"as a striking evidence of the approbation and interposition of Divine
Providence, we are informed by the great Jewish historian Josephus that,
although more than seven years were occupied in its building, yet during
the whole term it did not rain in the day time, but in the night season
.
only, that the workmen might not be obstructed from their labors."
In writing this, it would appear that Webb did not trouble to check with
a copy of the Josephus work directly, but only quoted from memory. And,
as a matter of fact, Josephus does say, in a translation of his The Anti. .
quities of the Jews, Book XV, Chapter .XI:
"It is also reported that during the time that the temple was bmldmg,
it did not rain in the day time, but that the showers fell in the nights, so
that the work was not hindered."
Here, it may be noted, the "seven years" required in building is not
specifically mentioned, but this may be taken to be only a mi.nor infract~on,
in a quotation presumably quoted from memory. But what is most senous
is that this verbatim quotation from Josephus, in Ch. XI, carries the
explanatory chapter-heading: "How Herod built the Temple." In other
words, Josephus was not describing the building of King Solomon's Temple
at all, at this point, but only of King Herod's Temple, the Third Temple,
built a thousand years later!
This error, in the 1805 Edition, has been carried through without change
in all the further editions of Webb's work, as well as in the Monitors that
came after him, with some exceptions where the error had apparently
been detected and rectified by omission, on the basis that, since the
Josephus quotation refers to an account of the building of King Herod's
Temple, it does not belong in a Monitorial description devoted to King
Solomon's Temple. Based on this reasoning,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the following instruction be adopted and sent to all Lodges in this Jurisdiction, making reference to p. 34 of the Monitor, and striking out the section in the 12th line
thereof, beginning with "and as a striking evidence" and ending with
"obstructed from their labors." And that in all future re-prints of our
Monitor, the above passage, herein deleted, shall be omitted.

DELETION FROM MONITOR AND OFFICERS' MANUAL
(2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it is possibly well known to most Masters and other Lodge
Officers that our present Monitor is based on The Freemason's Monitor,
or Illustrations of Masonry, by Thomas Smith Webb, first published in
Albany, N.Y. in 1797 (with numerous revised editions thereafter). This
American work was in turn based (largely verbatim) upon The Illustrations of Masonry, by William Preston, published under Grand Lodge
auspices in London in 1772, thus bringing our Monitorial work in line
with the practice in England.
In the 1805 Third Edition of Webb's work, a curious error appears
which had not previously appeared in the earlier editions, or in Preston.

WEARING OF MODIFIED APRONS-FORMER INSPECTORS

(4)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 1108a provides for the Grand Secretary to supply
each Inspector with an Inspector's Apron, said Apron to become the
personal property of the Inspector; and
WHEREAS, the average length of service to this Grand Lodge as
Inspectors exceeds five years, and
WHEREAS, there presently is no provision for the continued use of
these beautiful, attractive Aprons after these Inspectors resign and are
replaced.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that former Inspectors of
this Grand Jurisdiction who remain members in good standing, be permitted the continued use of these Aprons after slight modification, to
distinguish them from present Inspectors (such modification costs to be
borne by the individual former Inspector). Said modification being thus:
in the lower right corner in the light blue field, one half inch from side
and bottom of gold edging, using dark blue thread the same color as the
dark blue border; embroider two (2) 1 inch high numbers designating the
last year served as an Inspector.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that former Inspectors be permitted
to purchase replacement Inspectors' Aprons (without modification) at the
then current established price through the Grand Secretary's office.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the required amendments be made
to the appropriate section(s) of the California Masonic Code, as determined by the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 4 would allow former Inspectors to retain their Inspector's Aprons and wear them when appropriate modifications are made.
The modification of each apron would be at the former Inspector's expense
and would consist of embroidering the last year the Inspector served at
the lower right hand edge of the apron.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is not unmindful of
the time and dedication of the Inspectors of this Jurisdiction, and a desire
by the Brethren to recognize this devotion. However, to create an additional form of apron would start a precedent whereby any person serving
in Grand Lodge upon conclusion of his term could seek a Grand Lodge
apron "with appropriate modifications."
To allow the use of other than our recognized aprons could erode our
Masonic dress whereby eventually there would be unnecessary multiplicity.

are approved investments under the section.

d. Such evidences of corporate indebtedness as are rated "A:' or better
by Standard and Poors Corporation or Moody's Investors Service
and in shares of investment funds whose assets are limited to short
term United States Government securities, bank certificates of deposit, bankers' acceptances, commercial paper, repurchase agreements, and comparable securities. Except for United States Government securities, none of the securities shall have maturity dates in
excess of one year.

PERMIT RESIDENTS TO USE
ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGE~
MASONIC HOME, UNION CITY

(8)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, wine, one of the elements of Masonic Consecration, and
as a symbol of the inward refreshment of a good conscience, is intended

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

under the name of the "wine of refreshment," to remind us of the eternal
refreshments which the good are to receive in the future life for the faithful
performance of duty in the present, (from the Masonic Encyclopedia),
and
WHEREAS, at the present time, wine is used in the Dedication of
Masonic Halls Ceremony, and is referred to as a "comfort," and
WHEREAS, our Holy Bible recommends wine in moderation to "make
glad the heart," (Ps. 104: 15); "give wine to those of heavy heart," (Ps.
31:6); "use a little wine for stomach's sake," (I Tim. 5:23); and
WHEREAS, since 1933, when the 18th Amendment was repealed by
the 21st Amendment, allowing the use of wine to be an individual responsibility, and
WHEREAS, the residents of the Masonic Homes for the Aged are
either members of the Masonic Lodge, the Order of the Eastern Star,
both organizations requiring character investigation, or the wife or widow
of a Master Mason, who have turned over to the Masonic Homes of
California whatever assets he (or she) may be possessed or may become
possessed, and as this decision on their part is virtually irrevocable making
them absolutely dependent upon us, and
.
WHEREAS, we are charged with the responsibility of the complete
care, happiness and comfort of the residents of our Homes, and
WHEREAS, when these residents enter the doors of the Masonic
Homes, they are committed to living the remainder of their lives in
complete abstinence, although many have enjoyed drinking these beverages for years, and
WHEREAS,these Masonic Homes are the actual HOME of the residents and not a Masonic Temple, and
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code, Ordinance No. 2050, prohibits the serving of liquor, wine or beer in any building owned or operated
by a Masonic Lodge or any organization a prerequisite of membership
wherein is that a person be a Master Mason, and
WHEREAS, the word LIQUOR is defined by Webster's Third New
International Dictionary as: "a liquid substance, as: a. something drunk
as a beverage (as water, milk, fruit juice);" thus the serving of any water,
milk, fruit juice is also prohibited in any building owned or operated by
a Masonic Lodge, and
WHEREAS, the Masonic Order is dedicated to Brotherly Love, Relief
and Truth.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section No. 2050, page
97 of the California Masonic Code be corrected by deleting the words
"wine or beer" and replaced by inserting the words "containing alcohol".
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that following the words, "Master
Mason" the words "except the Masonic Homes for the Aged" be inserted.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that gift donations be used to finance
the supplying of these beverages to the residents so desiring.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes and to Masonic Homes Board of Trustees.

Respectfully submitted,
JOHN B. ALLEN, PM No. 95

WILLIAM L. ALLEN, M No. 95

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 8 was referred reports as follows:
This Resolution proposes that if residents of our Home for the Aged
desire a drink of spirituous, malt or fermented liquor it can be served to
them if they or the Masonic Homes have received gifts to be used for this
purpose. To carry out this proposal we submit the following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2050 of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows:
1. By substituting "spirituous, malt or fermented liquors" for "liquor,
wine or beer" in lines 5 and 8.
2. By inserting after "that" in line 7 the words "except as hereinafter
provided and"
3. By adding at the end of the Section "and provided further, that
spirituous, malt and fermented liquor may be possessed by our Home
for the Aged and the residents therein and may be used and served
at our Masonic Home for the Aged if purchased or acquired from
gifts to said Masonic Home for the Aged or the residents therein
specifically to be used for such purposes."
R_ESOLVED further, that Section 2048 of the C.M.C. be amended by
addmg at the end thereof the following: "This Section shall not prohibit
a Masonic Lodge, or an organization the prerequisite of membership
wherein is that a person be a Master Mason from holding a Stated or
special Meeting in the Masonic Home for the Aged."
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
foregoing resolutions.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution apparently proposes to do three things:
1) to change the definition contained in CMC Section 2050 from "liquor,
wine or beer" to "liquor containing alcohol,"
2) to allow liquor containing alcohol to be served at the "Masonic
Homes for the Aged,"
3) to use "gift donations" to finance the supplying of such beverages to
residents desiring them.
The main thrust of the resolution is the second thing stated above: to
allow alcoholic beverages to be served at the Home at Union City.
No statistics tell us how many Masons consume or do not consume
alcoholic beverages. Whatever the personal belief of members, however,
it has been the policy of Masonry in California to prohibit serving of
alcoholic beverages on property owned by a Lodge or Masonic-related
organization (see CMC, Section 2050). How can we make an exception

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for the people at the Home at Union City? Do we change a basic principle
because it is their home though owned by Grand Lodge? If so, how do we
then retain the principle?
Many people feel that one of the things which distinguishes Masonry
from other fraternal orders is the abstinence from serving alcoholic beverages. We believe that distinction is important, that the consequences of
a change would make of this a different organization and that no deviation
from the principle should be allowed for the Home at Union City.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "NO" vote.

LODGE SPONSORSHIP OF RAINBOW ASSEMBLIES

242

The Masonic Homes Board of Trustees:
The following reasons are presented toward a position of opposing the
resolution.
1. From the wording included in the resolution, there would be no
restriction on where the wine and beer could be consumed.
2. Those residents who would use any type of alcoholic beverage could
have license to consume it any time and in any amount and not be
inhibited about doing so anywhere.
3. If we were expected to serve it in the dining room, it would force us
to restrict the age of our waitresses to 18 and older.
4. We strongly believe it could lead to a pattern of unmanageable
behaviour and that it will create problems between residents. It will
require administrative staff spending time with problem drinkers.
Counseling with the individual and appeasing disturbed neighbors
will be needed.
5. From observation of those residents who have been on scheduled
group activities away from the Home, an estimated 65-75% of them
do not now drink beer or wine. It is suggested that this same percentage would prevail in the existing population at the Home. Many
of them would have concern for their safety if it became permissable
to use alcoholic beverages in an unrestricted situation.
6. The resolution suggests that this activity be funded by gift donations.
We would be required to provide a special budget for its purchase.
To support such a budget we would be in competition with requests
for contributions to our Masonic Homes Endowment Fund as well
as the Foundation.
The Masonic Homes Board of Trustees believe this resolution is not in
the best interests of the Masonic Home at Union City, and we strongly
recommend a "NO" vote.
Not Adopted.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this resolution has been
referred, reports as follows:

244

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The proponents of Resolution No. 9 seek to amend the California
Masonic Code to permit a Master Masons Lodge to sponsor not only one
or more Chapters of the Order of DeMolay, as at present, but also one
or more Assemblies of the International Order of Rainbow for Girls.
The proponents have also recently agreed that a Lodge should likewise
be permitted to sponsor one or more Bethels of the International Order
of Job's Daughters, in order that Grand Lodge may be consistent in its
relations with all Masonic youth orders. The proponents take note that
the statutes of the International Order of Job's Daughters now provide
for self-sponsorship only.
This enlargement of the original proposal becomes emergent legislation.
We therefore move that this report of the Jurisprudence Committee and
the proposed legislation to carry Resolution No. 9 into effect be received
as an emergent matter (if carried by 5/6 vote).
To carry out the full intent of the proponents, your Committee submits
the following legislation:
RESOLVED that Annotation 2070m be placed under Section 2316 of
the California Masonic Code, and be renumbered 2316o.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Annotation 2316p be added, reading as follows:
2316 p. Sponsoring of Rainbow for Girls and Job's Daughters. A Lodge
by resolution may sponsor an Assembly or Assemblies of the International
Order of Rainbow for Girls and a Bethel or Bethels of the International
Order of Job's Daughters - provided that the Constitution and Statutes
of the particular youth order permit such sponsorship.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
this resolution.

For this reason your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "YES" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 9 would permit a Lodge by resolution to sponsor a
Rainbow Assembly or Assemblies or Job's Daughters Bethel a well as a
DeMolay Chapter or Chapters.
Annotation 2070m permitting a Lodge to sponsor a Chapter or Chapters
of DeMolay is the result of a recommendation by Raymond A. Ebbage,
Grand Master in 1974. In his Message at 1974 Annual Communication
(Proceedings page 37) he stated, "I cannot emphasize too strongly the
urgent need for the sponsorship of DeMolay by our Lodges, and your
active support of the Job's Daughters and Rainbow groups."
Individual Bethel Councils of Job's Daughters are responsible to Grand
Bethel and are not sponsored by Lodges or Eastern Star Chapters. By
this resolution Bethels could be sponsored by a Lodge if permitted by
Grand Bethel. Rainbow Assemblies are usually sponsored by an Eastern
Star Chapter. Occasionally, however, there is not an Eastern Star Chapter
available to sponsor a Rainbow Assembly, and individual Masons and
Eastern Star members have assumed sponsorship or the Assembly has
ceased to exist. It is in the event that an Assembly does not have an
Eastern Star Chapter sponsor that it would be desirable for a Lodge to
assume sponsorship.

245

The Committee on Youth Orders:
The Grand Lodge of California, as indicated in the resolution, has
continually encouraged support for the youth of our country; and specifically for our Masonic Affiliated Youth Orders-The International Orders
of DeMolay, Job's Daughters, and the Rainbow for Girls.
The Youth Orders Committee commends the Brethren of John D.
Spreckels Lodge No. 657 for their concern and interest in our youth.
However, it must be asked why limit sponsorship to only two of our
Masonic Affiliated Youth groups? The omission of the International Order
of Job's Daughters is perhaps intentional as they do not recognize, at the
present time, any sponsors for their organization. Yet it is possible that
this may change in the future.
My Brethren, the line dividing support from sponsorship is a thin one;
and in fact, the two terms are generally considered synonymous for all
practical purposes. Traditionally, in this Jurisdiction, the Masonic Lodges
have supported all three of our youth groups. Only recently, since the
1972 Annual Communication has it been possible for Masonic Lodges to
sponsor DeMolay Chapters. Up to this point in time it has not been
deemed necessary for this Grand Lodge to allow our constituent Lodges
to sponsor either of the other two organizations. Eastern Star chapters
have traditionally sponsored Rainbow Assemblies and Job's Daughters
Bethels, as indicated, have no sponsors. However now, my Brethren, our
Masonic Affiliated Youth Orders are in desperate straits; their membership
rolls are down by more than 50%, but their prime lack is adult leadership .
Anything whiclt will promote more adult leadership and support would
be greatly appreciated by them. Allowing Lodge sponsorship would be a
step in the right direction. This is not to detract from the efforts of Eastern
Star Chapters who are doing a superb job in sponsoring Rainbow Assemblies, nor to the lack of sponsorship of Job's Daughters Bethels. Rather,
it would be to provide another avenue for Masonic leadership and participation. It is therefore deemed appropriate that our constituent Lodges
be authorized to sponsor any of our Masonic Affiliated Youth groups if
the governing body of the particular youth group permits such sponsorship.
RECOMMENDATION: It is recommended that the final paragraph of
Resolution No. 9 be ammended to read as follows:
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2070m, of the
California Masonic Code be ammended to read:
"2070m. Sponsoring of Masonic Affiliated Youth Groups. A Lodge by
resolution may sponsor a Chapter or Chapters of DeMolay, and/or an
Assembly or Assemblies of the International Order of the Rainbow for
Girls and/or a Bethel or Bethels of the International Order of Job's
Daughters provided the Constitution and statutes of the particular youth
order permit such sponsorship."

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to amend Sections 2318 and

"Except as otherwise prohibited by this Code, Lodges may plan and
finance local programs and activities compatible with Masonic values
and traditions."
To place the matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution would grant authority to Lodges to plan and finance
local activities which would be "socially visible" and "compatible with
Masonic values and traditions."
Section 2316 of our Masonic Code governs use of funds for necessary
expenses of the Lodge and for special calls for charity. The section further
provides the Lodge shall not use funds or property for any purposes except
those permitted by the Code.
Section 2318 states that the expenditure of funds for any program required by the Grand Lodge, or the Grand Master, shall be deemed to be
part of the necessary expenses of the Lodge, and sets out restrictions upon
expenditures fo~ Public Schools Week and Constitution Observances.
The thrust of the Masonic Code limitations is to limit expenditures
closely. Individual charity to members is ~:me of the pri~e .goals ~f .Masonry. But charity by Lodges to those outside the Fraternity is. pro~ibite~.
However, Masons as individuals are encouraged to be active m their
communities and their private charities.
Attempts have been made in the past by Lodges to engage in visible
activities. For example, Annotation 2316j (1956) of the California Masonic
Code provides that a parade float or vehicle cannot be financed or sponsored from Lodge funds.
Why should such limitations ever have been the rule? Are those reasons
.
enough to warrant their continued existence?
One effect of such limitations is to allow dues to remam low. A small
effort by an average Lodge to "be visible" could serio.usly affect the need
for additional dues. In the average Lodge the expenditure of $1500 could
.
raise dues by $5.00!
How should we operate? As we have, an organization known by its
members and their private contributions to visible activities, or as an
organization which itself makes such contributions?
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "NO" vote.
Not Adopted.

REDUCE AGE MINIMUM-DE MOLAY MEMBERS

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 13 proposes to amend Section 2636 CMC to permit
members of the Order of DeMolay to petition Masonic Lodges for membership at the age of eighteen (18).
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes sympathizes with the
proponents of this Resolution in their interest in the Order of DeMolay.
However, your Committee is concerned with the effect this proposed
legislation would have on the Order of DeMolay. A DeMolay remains
such until his twenty-first (21) birthday. If he became a Master Mason at
the age of eighteen (18) would he then lose his interest and cease being
active in DeMolay? If so, this would create a very serious negative effect,
because DeMolay survives on the continued support and efforts of these
young men until they arrive at the age of twenty-one (21).
This Resolution proposes to establish preferential treatment to members
of the Order of DeMolay and many of their respected leaders have spoken
out against such preferential treatment, stating that DeMolays desire to
approach membership in the Masonic Fraternity on the same basis as have
all those who have gone before.
It is the opinion of your Committee that if it is desirable to reduce the
age limit for DeMolays, it should also be desirable to similarly accept all
applicants of the same age. To limit the age reduction to DeMolay only
would create two classes of applicants and your Committee believes this
to be contrary to our Masonic principles and the policy of this Grand
Lodge. Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a
"NO" vote.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution proposes that an applicant for the degrees of Masonry
from a qualified resident of this Grand Jurisdiction be required to petition
the Lodge nearest his place of residence; and that if the applicant wishes
to apply to another Lodge other than in the area in which he lives, he
must first secure a release or waiver of jurisdiction from the Lodge nearest
where he lives.
In this day and age a great many people work and spend a very large
part of each day in areas distant from their residences; and an applicant
for the degrees of Masonry might well desire to petition a Lodge near his
place of employment or where his friends work or live, even though it be
a great distance from his residence. To require such an applicant to first
obtain a release or waiver of jurisdiction from the Lodge closest to where
he lives would place an undue burden and hardship upon the applicant.
Membership, of course, is important to all Lodges, but the desire and
convenience of the applicant should take priority in this instance.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "NO"
vote.
